* 10 November ''Dead Men Talk'', new dating techniques reveal more about the evolution of man, found from the [[Skhul and Qafzeh hominins]] at the [[Qafzeh cave]], and future DNA sequencing methods could reveal from bones how man evolved, it featured Milford H. Wolpoff and Chris Stringer, being similar to the September 1996 edition about Neanderthals; a cave object was thought to be 40,000 years ago, but now was thought to be 100,000 years old; there were two paradigms, one where everyone is from Homo Erectus, and the other where Homo Sapiens evolved exclusively in Africa from Homo Erectus; this theory was from evidence at Border Cave in South Africa, [[Omo Kibish Formation]] in Ethiopia, and the Skhul cave; Milford Wolpoff, of the University of Michigan, supported the first multi-regional model; the second Eve theory came from Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum, who looked at a fossil at [[Jebel Irhoud]], Morocco; new dating techniques were [[electron spin resonance dating]] (ESR), deployed by Dr Rainer Grün at the [[Godwin Laboratory, University of Cambridge]], and [[thermoluminescence dating]] (TL) which looked at flints that had been heated in primitive fires; a Neanderthal at [[Kebara Cave]] was dated at 60,000, with the new dating technique; the two caves, Skhul had homo sapiens, and [[Tanum Cave]] had Neanderthals, nearby; Chris Stringer thought that the Neanderthals split 300,000 years ago; the Neanderthal found at [[Amud Cave]] had a large brain; Joel Rak of [[Tel Aviv University]] believed that Neanderthals were a separate species; geneticist [[Rebecca L. Cann]], of the University of California, Berkeley, was the first to look at the genetics of mitochondria, passed along the female line; this led to the Mitochondrial Eve theory, who was thought to have lived 200,000 years ago; the new PCR technique allowed strands of hair to be genetically sequenced; [[Anna Di Rienzo]] developed the mitochondrial genetics technique at Berkeley, and dated Homo Sapiens to have left Africa around 100,000 years ago; the Cro-Magnon appeared in Eastern Europe 40,000 years ago, who were the first to eat fish; Paul Mellars of University of Cambridge; the [[Vézère]] valley in France, with a [[Cro-Magnon]] cave, from the upper palaeolithic era; [[Lawrence H. * 10 October ''In the Path of a Killer Volcano'', with seismologists Dave Harlow, [[Richard Hoblitt]], and John Ewert of the [[United States Geological Survey]]; although the biggest volcanic explosion since Krakatoa was about to occur, the seismologists at [[Philippine Institute of Volcanology, and Seismology]] (PHIVOLCS) and its director [[Ray Punongbayan]], were mostly totally unaware of anything that abnormal; PHIVOLCS put a [[seismometer]] near the volcano, and it recorded over 400 earthquakes in just two days near the summit, so Ray Punongbayan requested urgent assistance from the US Geological Survey; [[Clark Air Base]] and [[U.S. Naval Base Subic Bay]] were around ten miles away, so seven seismic stations were in place by early May; a helicopter was flown around the site and air samples were taken for a correlation spectrometer to detect any sulphur dioxide, with [[Ultraviolet–visible spectroscopy|the ultraviolet]]; [[Christopher G. the Royal Society gave him a research fellowship to work at Imperial College; as further exploratory work was clocked up, with calculations inclya variable speed of light, the team of physicists looked at other applications for their controversial proposals, such as the flatness problem, and what happened before the Big Bang; in 1998 astrophysicist John Webb, at the University of Cambridge, worked on the theory of a variable speed of light, through investigating [[quasar]]s, the most distant objects that can be seen; and by looking at supernovae, it was largely expected that any recorded data would show indications of a deceleration in the rate of expansion of the universe, but the data instead showed that the rate of expansion was - increasing, which led to the [[lambda-CDM model]]. * 15 July ''Saving the Leaning Tower'', a documentary chronicling the dramatic rescue of one of the world’s most iconic landmarks. By the late 1980s, the [[Leaning Tower of Pisa]] was on the brink of collapse, its southward tilt increasing steadily and threatening catastrophic failure. Alarm spread after the sudden fall of a medieval bell tower in [[Pavia]] in 1989, which convinced authorities to close [[Pisa]]’s monument to the public. An international committee of engineers, geologists, and historians was formed to save the tower, among them British civil engineer [[John Burland]]. Through detailed investigation, the team uncovered the structural weaknesses behind the marble façade and the unstable soils beneath Pisa. Computer models showed the tower should already have collapsed. Temporary steel tendons and 600 tonnes of lead counterweights prevented immediate disaster, but the tower’s fate remained uncertain. Burland proposed a novel, delicate solution: controlled “soil extraction” below the northern side to allow the tower to gently tilt back to stability. The project was plagued by risks, political disputes, and near-disasters, including the “Black September” of 1995, when freezing the foundations caused the tower to lurch alarmingly. Despite opposition, the soil extraction method was eventually approved in 1998. Over two years, engineers removed around 70 tonnes of soil, gradually reducing the lean by half a meter without visible alteration to the monument. By June 2001, the tower had been successfully stabilized, restored to the inclination it had in the 18th century, and reopened to the public. The operation was hailed as one of the greatest feats of modern civil engineering, ensuring the survival of Pisa’s unique heritage for centuries to come. The documentary presents not only the technical challenges but also the cultural, historical, and emotional significance of preserving this medieval masterpiece.

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Machiavellianism (psychology)
======================================================================

{{short description|Personality construct}}
{{About|the psychology construct assigned the name Machiavellianism|the political philosophy of Machiavelli|Machiavellianism (politics)}}
[[File:The Dark Triad.svg|right|thumb|Machiavellianism is one of the traits in the dark triad model, along with psychopathy and narcissism.]]

In the field of [[personality psychology]], '''Machiavellianism''' (sometimes abbreviated as '''MACH''') is the name of a personality trait construct characterized by [[Manipulation_(psychology)|manipulativeness]], indifference to [[morality]], lack of empathy, and a calculated focus on [[self-interest]].<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-174450-2.50010-5 |chapter=In Search of the Machiavel |title=Studies in Machiavellianism |date=1970 |last1=Geis |first1=Florence |last2=Christie |first2=Richard |last3=Nelson |first3=Carnot |page=76 |isbn=978-0-12-174450-2}}</ref><ref name="Jones-2009a">{{cite book |last1=Jones |first1=Daniel N. |last2=Paulhus |first2=Delroy L. |chapter=Machiavellianism |pages=93–108 |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VgcGZ5sCEcIC&pg=PA93 |editor1-last=Leary |editor1-first=Mark R. |editor2-last=Hoyle |editor2-first=Rick H. |title=Handbook of Individual Differences in Social Behavior |date=2009 |publisher=Guilford Press |isbn=978-1-59385-647-2}}</ref><ref> 
*"In sum, the key elements of Machiavellianism appear to be (a) manipulativeness, (b) callous affect, and (c) a strategic-calculating orientation." —-{{harvnb|Jones|Paulhus|2014}}
*{{cite journal |last1=Furnham |first1=Adrian |last2=Treglown |first2=Luke |title=The Dark Side of High-Fliers: The Dark Triad, High-Flier Traits, Engagement, and Subjective Success |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |date=27 April 2021 |volume=12 |article-number=647676 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2021.647676 |doi-access=free |pmid=33986711 |pmc=8110703 }}</ref><ref name="Jones Figueredo Core of Darkness">{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Daniel Nelson |last2=Figueredo |first2=Aurelio Jose |title=The Core of Darkness: Uncovering the Heart of the Dark Triad |journal=European Journal of Personality |date=November 2013 |volume=27 |issue=6 |pages=521–531 |doi=10.1002/per.1893 }}</ref> Psychologists [[Richard Christie (psychologist)|Richard Christie]] and [[Florence L. Geis]] created the construct in the 1960s. They devised a set of statements to study variations in human behaviors and named it after [[Niccolò Machiavelli]].{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=10, 339}}<ref name="Colman-2015">{{cite book |last1=Colman |first1=Andrew M. |chapter=Machiavellianism |page=434 |chapter-url={{GBurl|UDnvBQAAQBAJ |p=434}} |title=A Dictionary of Psychology |date=2015 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-965768-1}}</ref><ref name="Rauthmann-2011">{{cite journal |last1=Rauthmann |first1=John F. |last2=Will |first2=Theresa |title=Proposing a Multidimensional Machiavellianism Conceptualization |journal=Social Behavior and Personality |date=30 April 2011 |volume=39 |issue=3 |pages=391–403 |doi=10.2224/sbp.2011.39.3.391|doi-access=free }}</ref> The construct has no relation to the historical figure outside of bearing his name.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9781315454818 |title=Counterproductive Work Behaviors |date=2018 |last1=Cohen |first1=Aaron |isbn=978-1-315-45481-8 |page=121 }}</ref>  Their ''[[MACH-IV (test)|Mach IV]]'' test, a 20-question, [[Likert Scale|Likert-scale]] [[Personality test|personality survey]], became the standard self-assessment tool and scale of the Machiavellianism construct. Those who score high on the scale (High Machs) are more likely to have a high level of [[Deception|deceitfulness]], exploitativeness and a cold, unemotional temperament.{{sfn|Spielberger|Butcher|2013|}}<ref name="Geis-1978">{{cite book |last1=Geis |first1=F. L. |chapter=Machiavellianism |pages=305–363 |editor1-last=London |editor1-first=Harvey |editor2-last=Exner |editor2-first=John E. |title=Dimensions of Personality |date=1978 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=978-0-471-54392-3}}</ref>

It is one of the [[dark triad]] traits, along with the [[wikt:subclinical|subclinical]] versions of [[narcissism]] and [[psychopathy]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Paulhus |first1=Delroy L |last2=Williams |first2=Kevin M |title=The Dark Triad of personality: Narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy |journal=Journal of Research in Personality |date=December 2002 |volume=36 |issue=6 |pages=556–563 |doi=10.1016/S0092-6566(02)00505-6 }}</ref>{{sfn|Lyons|2019|p=2}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Furnham |first1=Adrian |last2=Richards |first2=Steven C. |last3=Paulhus |first3=Delroy L. |title=The Dark Triad of Personality: A 10 Year Review |journal=Social and Personality Psychology Compass |date=March 2013 |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=199–216 |doi=10.1111/spc3.12018}}</ref>

==Origin of the construct==

===The creation of a manipulation scale===

In 1955, psychologist Richard Christie set out to study the thought processes and actions of those who manipulated others, such as political [[ideologues]] and [[religious extremists]].{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|pp=2–6}} He found that there was much literature on those who followed organizations and movements, but very little on those who led them. He began by conceptualizing what qualities a potential manipulator would have, such as a lack of empathy and affect, and being unconcerned with moral standards. Then as Christie was developing a psychometric for interpersonal manipulation, he thought it necessary to utilize the style of the various authors he was researching to better suit the needs of the construction of the test.<ref>See the chapter "Why Machiavelli" in Studies in Machiavellianism, 1970. pages 1-9</ref> In the 1960s, Christie and his colleagues would then develop a test using a selection of their own statements which they viewed were discriminatory enough to measure personality differences, naming the construct "Machiavellianism".<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-174450-2.50007-5 |chapter=Scale Construction |title=Studies in Machiavellianism |date=1970 |last1=Christie |first1=Richard |pages=10–34 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-12-174450-2}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-174450-2.50022-1 |chapter=Implications and Speculations |title=Studies in Machiavellianism |date=1970b |last1=Christie |first1=Richard |last2=Geis |first2=Florence |pages=339–358 |isbn=978-0-12-174450-2}}</ref><ref name="Jones-2009a"/>  They wanted to assess whether or not those who were in agreement with the statements would behave differently than others who disagreed, specifically in regards to manipulative actions. Christie and his research partner Florence L. Geis published their results in their book, titled "''[[Studies in Machiavellianism]]''", in 1970.<ref>{{cite thesis |id={{CORE output|222805824}} |last1=Monaghan |first1=C |date=2019 |title=Two-Dimensional Machiavellianism: Conceptualisation, Measurement, and Well-Being |quote=Despite such popular uses of concepts from Machiavelli, 'Machiavellianism', as a concept in psychology, was not formulated until 1970. }}</ref> 

The test items used were their own statements which they viewed Machiavelli could say, and were not direct statements from his works.{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=8-10}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shafer |first1=William E. |last2=Simmons |first2=Richard S. |title=Social responsibility, Machiavellianism and tax avoidance: A study of Hong Kong tax professionals |journal=Accounting, Auditing & Accountability Journal |date=20 June 2008 |volume=21 |issue=5 |pages=695–720 |doi=10.1108/09513570810872978 |quote=The Machiavellianism scale was initially developed by assembling a list of items believed to be theoretically congruent with arguments taken from Niccolo Machiavelli's The Prince and The Discourses. }}</ref>

===On the name of the scale===

While the construct is named "Machiavellianism", it does not refer to the political theory espoused in Machiavelli's books (also called [[Machiavellianism (politics)|Machiavellianism]]).<ref name="Laakasuo">"Note that the definition of Machiavellianism in psychology is simply a collection of specific traits (a person being cold, calculating, etc.). This is different from how the term has been used in, e.g., political theory." 
* Laakasuo, M., Sundvall, J. R., Berg, A., Drosinou, M., Herzon, V., Kunnari, A., ... & Palomäki, J. (2021). Moral psychology and artificial agents (Part two): The transhuman connection. In Machine law, ethics, and morality in the age of artificial intelligence (pp. 189-204). IGI Global.
</ref><ref>"...The Machiavellian personality in Mach-IV has little, if anything, to do with Machiavelli, either the man or his work."
* Cohen, A. (2018). Counterproductive work behaviors: Understanding the dark side of personalities in organizational Life. Routledge. [https://books.google.com/books?id=nClKDwAAQBAJ&pg=RA3-PT121 pg 121]</ref><ref name="Matthews">{{cite journal |last1=Matthews |first1=Michael J. |last2=Kelemen |first2=Thomas K. |last3=Matthews |first3=Samuel H. |last4=Matthews |first4=Jacob M. |title=The Machiavellian Organization: A Multilevel Model to Understand Decision Making in Organizations |journal=Group & Organization Management |date=April 2022 |volume=47 |issue=2 |pages=413–439 |doi=10.1177/10596011221081281 |quote=It is important to note the vast conceptual divergence between 'Machiavellianism' within psychology and 'Machiavellianism' within political theory or philosophy }}</ref><ref name="Hartley">{{cite book |last1=Hartley |first1=Dale |title=Machiavellians: Gulling the Rubes |date=2023 |isbn=979-8-223-34675-3 |page=2|publisher=Draft2digital|quote= When psychologists refer to the terms, ''Machiavellian'' or ''Machiavellianism'', they do not mean Machiavelli's political advice. They refer instead to the underlying personality traits of cynicism, duplicity and scheming by which master manipulators conceive and execute their agendas.}}</ref><ref name="Richford">"Because of the reactivity association with its nomenclature, the personality orientation, Machiavellianism, has frequently been confused with a political philosophy which is in conflict with democratic principles."
* Richford, M. (1981). [https://vtechworks.lib.vt.edu/items/7d7c2365-8dd3-4f38-9107-93eb8e269d8c A study of the Machiavellian orientation locus of control and job satisfaction of a selected sample of Virginia public school secondary level principals.]</ref> Because the two concepts share the same name, they can be confused for and conflated with one another, even though his political ideas are not relevant to psychology.<ref name="Richford"/><ref name="Cohen">Cohen, A. (2018). Counterproductive work behaviors: Understanding the dark side of personalities in organizational Life. Routledge. [https://books.google.com/books?id=nClKDwAAQBAJ&pg=RA3-PT121 pg 121]</ref><ref name="Hartley"/><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-981-19-4598-4_6 |chapter=Manipulative Social Behavior and Personality Disposition |title=Nature and Dynamics of Social Influence |date=2022 |last1=Pandey |first1=Janak |pages=125–152 |isbn=978-981-19-4597-7 }}</ref> Scholars have asserted that the variable has no relation to Machiavelli outside of bearing his name, and that it has nothing to do with Machiavelli's politics.<ref name="Cohen"/> Christie himself makes clear that he used sentences inspired by Machiavelli's works only as a sort of litmus test to study deceptive and manipulative behavior, and that his concern was not with Machiavelli's historical or political influence, stating specifically that:{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=1}}

<blockquote>  Historians disagree as to whether Machiavelli was a cynic who wrote political satire, a patriot, or the first modern political scientist. '''The present concern is not with Machiavelli as an historic figure, but as the source of ideas about those who manipulate others.''' </blockquote>

Christie stated that he chose the name "Machiavellianism" out of convenience seeing as other names such as "M scale" (M for manipulation) and "Ma scale" (which was used by the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory for [[hypomania]]) were taken. Names also considered were the "manipulator" or "operator"  scale, but these terms had issues regarding behavioral validity. He also accepts that by using the name "Machiavellianism", the scale would "create problems of public misunderstanding" due to the pre-existing political meaning of the term.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Christie |first1=R. |last2=Merton |first2=R. K. |title=Procedures for the sociological study of the values climate of medical schools |journal=Journal of Medical Education |date=October 1958 |volume=33 |issue=10 Part 2 |pages=125–153 |pmid=13588289 |quote=Abbreviations are not readily found; psychological jargon has already stamped a simple M as the term for movement response on the Rorschach, Ma has been preempted for the hypomania scale on the Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory }}</ref> In a later essay, Christie even states that some have viewed the name problematic and that "the use of the word ''Machiavellianism'' to describe the content of the scales has been questioned".<ref>Christie, R. Geis, F. "Some Consequences with Taking Machiavelli Seriously" in Edgar F. Borgatta and William W. Lambert (eds.). Handbook of Personality Theory and Research</ref> Many have called for the concept to be renamed entirely.<ref>{{cite book | last1=Pervin | first1=Lawrence A. | last2=John | first2=Oliver P. | title=Handbook of Personality, Second Edition: Theory and Research | date=18 August 1999 | publisher=Guilford Publications | isbn=978-1-57230-483-3 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ByCQzQEACAAJ&q=Handbook+of+Personality+Theory+and+Research }}</ref>{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|pp=339}}

===''MACH-IV''===
Christie and Geis's ''MACH IV'' test, a 20-question, [[Likert Scale|Likert-scale]] personality survey, became the standard self-report tool to measure one's level of Machiavellianism.<ref name="Colman-2015"/> Those who score highly on the scale are classified as ''high Machs'', while those who score low are classified as ''low Machs''.<ref name="Jones-2009a"/> "Machiavellian" is also used but has a far more technical use in this context, and has been adopted by psychologists to refer to this scale and those who score high on it.<ref>
* "The terms ''dark personalities,'' ''narcissists,'' ''Machiavellians,'' and ''psychopaths'' are ''not'' used as diagnostic labels, but as abbreviations only for people scoring (highly) on respective personality dimensions. Further, no pathology is implied; the terms are solely used for subclinical forms of the respective personality dimensions"----Rauthmann, J. F. (2012). The Dark Triad and interpersonal perception: Similarities and differences in the social consequences of narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 3(4), 487-496.
* Furtner, M. R., Maran, T., & Rauthmann, J. F. (2017). Dark leadership: The role of leaders' dark triad personality traits. Leader development deconstructed, 75-99.
*"Machiavellians—individuals who have high scores on Mach scales—display a specific emotion regulation style."----Deak, A., Bodrogi, B., Biro, B., Perlaki, G., Orsi, G., & Bereczkei, T. (2017). Machiavellian emotion regulation in a cognitive reappraisal task: An fMRI study. Cognitive, Affective, & Behavioral Neuroscience, 17, 528-541.
* "Individuals with high scores on Mach scales—that is "high Machs" (HM) in short or "Machiavellians"—have a tendency to be callous, selfish, and malevolent in their interpersonal dealings." ------Bereczkei, T., Szabo, Z. P., & Czibor, A. (2015). Abusing good intentions: Machiavellians strive for exploiting cooperators. SAGE Open, 5(2), 2158244015593119.
* "According to research conducted on the Machiavellianism scale, respondents with high scores on a Machiavellianism scale are titled as Machiavellians or high Machs; those with low scores on the scale have been called non-Machiavellians or low Machs."--------- Crotts, J. C., Aziz, A., & Upchurch, R. S. (2005). Research note: Relationship between Machiavellianism and sales performance. Tourism Analysis, 10(1), 79-84.
* "The term Machiavellian is used here and hereafter not as a diagnosis or label, but as a term denoting someone who scores highly on Machiavellianism."--Rauthmann, J. F., & Will, T. (2011). Proposing a multidimensional Machiavellianism conceptualization. Social Behavior and Personality: an international journal, 39(3), 391-403.
</ref> Using their scale, Christie and Geis conducted multiple experimental tests that showed that the interpersonal approaches and behavior of "high Machs" and "low Machs" differ.{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=260}} People scoring high on the scale tend to endorse manipulative statements, and behave accordingly, contrary to those who score lowly.<ref name="EI"/> People scoring high on the scale tend to endorse statements such as, "Never tell anyone the real reason you did something unless it is useful to do so," (No. 1) but not ones like, "Most people are basically good and kind" (No. 4), "There is no excuse for lying to someone else" (No. 7) or "Most people who get ahead in the world lead clean, moral lives" (No. 11){{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|}} Their basic results have been widely replicated.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9780203488508-7 |chapter=Bypassing Empathy: A Machiavellian Theory of Mind and Sneaky Power |title=Individual Differences in Theory of Mind |date=2004 |pages=50–77 |isbn=978-0-203-48850-8 |first1=Doris |last1=McIlwain |publisher=Psychology Press |editor1-first=Betty |editor1-last=Repacholi |editor2-first=Virginia |editor2-last=Slaughter}}</ref> Measured on the ''Mach IV'' scale, males score, on average, slightly higher on Machiavellianism than females.{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=260}}<ref name="Gunnthorsdottir-2002">{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/S0167-4870(01)00067-8 |title=Using the Machiavellianism instrument to predict trustworthiness in a bargaining game |journal=Journal of Economic Psychology |volume=23 |pages=49–66 |year=2002 |last1=Gunnthorsdottir |first1=Anna |last2=McCabe |first2=Kevin |last3=Smith |first3=Vernon|issue=1 }}</ref>

The Mach IV test influenced the creation of an assessment called the Dirty Dozen, which contains 12 items, and the Short Dark Triad, composed of 27 items.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Muris |first1=Peter |last2=Merckelbach |first2=Harald |last3=Otgaar |first3=Henry |last4=Meijer |first4=Ewout |title=The Malevolent Side of Human Nature: A Meta-Analysis and Critical Review of the Literature on the Dark Triad (Narcissism, Machiavellianism, and Psychopathy) |journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science |date=March 2017 |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=183–204 |doi=10.1177/1745691616666070 |pmid=28346115 |url=https://cris.maastrichtuniversity.nl/en/publications/4f0f862e-6b3b-44d5-8134-5aadb21e4b7d }}</ref> The MACH-IV (and other Machiavellianism tests) also feature questions loosely inspired by other thinkers such as Chinese political authors.{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|pp=6}}<ref name="Jones-2009"/><ref name="Measures"/> 

'''High vs Low Machiavellianism'''

Like all personality traits, Machiavellianism is a characteristic that exists on a spectrum or continuum.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Belschak |first1=Frank D. |last2=Jacobs |first2=Gabriele |last3=Giessner |first3=Steffen R. |last4=Horton |first4=Kate E. |last5=Bayerl |first5=P. Saskia |title=When the going gets tough: Employee reactions to large-scale organizational change and the role of employee Machiavellianism |journal=Journal of Organizational Behavior |date=November 2020 |volume=41 |issue=9 |pages=830–850 |doi=10.1002/job.2478 |quote=Machiavellianism is defined as a quantitative personality trait, implying that individuals might score higher or lower on the continuum of Machiavellianism. |hdl=1765/129791 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hutter |first1=Katja |last2=Füller |first2=Johann |last3=Hautz |first3=Julia |last4=Bilgram |first4=Volker |last5=Matzler |first5=Kurt |title=Machiavellianism or Morality: Which Behavior Pays Off In Online Innovation Contests? |journal=Journal of Management Information Systems |date=3 July 2015 |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=197–228 |doi=10.1080/07421222.2015.1099181}}</ref><ref name="Monaghan-2016">{{cite journal |last1=Monaghan |first1=Conal |last2=Bizumic |first2=Boris |last3=Sellbom |first3=Martin |title=The role of Machiavellian views and tactics in psychopathology |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=May 2016 |volume=94 |pages=72–81 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2016.01.002}}</ref><ref>{{citation|quote="Machiavellianism is normally distributed in the general population and consequently, "Machiavellians" do not exist as a distinct category within society (nontaxonic; Beller & Bosse, 2017…" |doi=10.1037/pas0000784 |title=Two-dimensional Machiavellianism: Conceptualization, theory, and measurement of the views and tactics dimensions |date=2020 |last1=Monaghan |first1=Conal |last2=Bizumic |first2=Boris |last3=Williams |first3=Todd |last4=Sellbom |first4=Martin |journal=Psychological Assessment |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=277–293 |pmid=31750680 }}</ref> Christie and others noted that High Machs were more likely to cheat in experimental games, manipulate others around them, and were generally detached in their interactions. This was opposed to the behavior of Low Machs, who found such behaviors immoral, and refrained from them.{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=312}}

The higher a person is on the Machiavellianism scale, the more likely they are to deceive and exploit at the expense of someone else, engage in unprincipled behavior, and have a lack of empathetic feelings.<ref name="Jones-2009a"/>

==Core features==
In developing the construct, Christie theorized that a "manipulator" or "operator" would possess the following characteristics:{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=3}}

1. '''A relative lack of affect in interpersonal relationships''': Manipulators do not empathize with their victims. The more empathy one has, Christie says, the less likely one will manipulate a person to do their bidding.

2. '''A lack of concern for conventional morality''': Christie asserts that the manipulator is not concerned with the morality of behaviors such as lying and cheating.

3. '''A lack of gross [[Mental illness|psychopathology]]''': Christie states that manipulators usually have an instrumentalist view of the world, which shows a lack of psychosis or other mental impairments.

4. '''Low ideological commitment:''' Manipulators prefer to focus on getting things done pragmatically rather than focus on ideological allegiances. Christie states that while manipulators are to be found in organizations of differing ideals, they are more likely to be interested in tactics that achieve individual ends than inflexible idealistic ones.{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=3}}

===Five-Factor Model===
Under the Five-Factor Model of Machiavellianism, three characteristics underlie the construct:<ref name="Collison-2018">{{cite journal |last1=Collison |first1=Katherine L. |last2=Vize |first2=Colin E. |last3=Miller |first3=Joshua D. |last4=Lynam |first4=Donald R. |title=Development and preliminary validation of a five factor model measure of Machiavellianism |journal=Psychological Assessment |date=October 2018 |volume=30 |issue=10 |pages=1401–1407 |doi=10.1037/pas0000637 |pmid=30047746 |url=https://psyarxiv.com/teg8j/|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* '''Antagonism:''' manipulativeness, cynicism, selfishness, callousness, and arrogance.
* '''Planfulness:''' deliberation and orderliness.
* '''Agency:''' achievement-striving, [[assertiveness]], self-confidence, emotional invulnerability, activity and competence.

==Causes==
===Genetics and upbringing===
Several [[Behavioural genetics|behavioral genetics]] studies have shown that Machiavellianism has both significantly genetic and environmental influences.<ref name="Petrides-2011">{{cite journal |last1=Petrides |first1=K. V. |last2=Vernon |first2=Philip A. |last3=Schermer |first3=Julie Aitken |last4=Veselka |first4=Livia |title=Trait Emotional Intelligence and the Dark Triad Traits of Personality |journal=Twin Research and Human Genetics |date=February 2011 |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=35–41 |doi=10.1375/twin.14.1.35 |pmid=21314254}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2007.09.007 |title=A behavioral genetic investigation of the Dark Triad and the Big 5 |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=445–452 |year=2008 |last1=Vernon |first1=Philip A. |last2=Villani |first2=Vanessa C. |last3=Vickers |first3=Leanne C. |last4=Harris |first4=Julie Aitken}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Furnham |first1=Adrian |last2=Richards |first2=Steven C. |last3=Paulhus |first3=Delroy L. |title=The Dark Triad of Personality: A 10 Year Review |journal=Social and Personality Psychology Compass |date=March 2013 |volume=7 |issue=3 |pages=199–216 |doi=10.1111/spc3.12018 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Veselka |first1=Livia |last2=Schermer |first2=Julie Aitken |last3=Vernon |first3=Philip A. |title=Beyond the Big Five: The Dark Triad and the Supernumerary Personality Inventory |journal=Twin Research and Human Genetics |date=April 2011 |volume=14 |issue=2 |pages=158–168 |doi=10.1375/twin.14.2.158 |pmid=21425898}}</ref> Researchers have noted that while Machiavellianism is heritable to a substantial degree, it can also be influenced by the shared-environment (i.e. sibling groups) slightly more than narcissism and psychopathy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Monaghan |first1=Conal |last2=Bizumic |first2=Boris |last3=Sellbom |first3=Martin |title=Nomological network of two-dimensional Machiavellianism |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=August 2018 |volume=130 |pages=161–173 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2018.03.047 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Petrides |first1=K. V. |last2=Vernon |first2=Philip A. |last3=Schermer |first3=Julie Aitken |last4=Veselka |first4=Livia |title=Trait Emotional Intelligence and the Dark Triad Traits of Personality |journal=Twin Research and Human Genetics |date=February 2011 |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=35–41 |doi=10.1375/twin.14.1.35 |pmid=21314254 }}</ref> Other traits associated with Machiavellianism are influenced by genetics as well, as one study notes that "The co-occurrence of [[alexithymia]] and Machiavellianism was most heavily influenced by genetic factors, and to a lesser but significant extent by non-shared environmental factors."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cairncross |first1=Molly |last2=Veselka |first2=Livia |last3=Schermer |first3=Julie Aitken |last4=Vernon |first4=Philip A. |title=A Behavioral Genetic Analysis of Alexithymia and the Dark Triad Traits of Personality |journal=Twin Research and Human Genetics |date=June 2013 |volume=16 |issue=3 |pages=690–697 |doi=10.1017/thg.2013.19 |pmid=23561050 }}</ref> Machiavellianism is also heavily correlated with primary psychopathy which is itself strongly heritable.<ref name="Bereczkei-2015">{{cite journal |last1=Bereczkei |first1=Tamas |title=The manipulative skill: Cognitive devices and their neural correlates underlying Machiavellian's decision making |journal=Brain and Cognition |date=October 2015 |volume=99 |pages=24–31 |doi=10.1016/j.bandc.2015.06.007 |pmid=26189112}}</ref> A study on the "core" of dark triad traits also emphasized that the residual traits of Machiavellianism had "significant genetic components".<ref name="Schermer-2020">{{cite journal |last1=Schermer |first1=Julie Aitken |last2=Jones |first2=Daniel N. |title=The behavioral genetics of the dark triad core versus unique trait components: A pilot study |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=February 2020 |volume=154 |article-number=109701 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2019.109701}}</ref> The relationship between Machiavellianism and mental toughness is also moderated by environmental factors and a genetic basis.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Onley |first1=Michael |last2=Veselka |first2=Livia |last3=Schermer |first3=Julie Aitken |last4=Vernon |first4=Philip A. |title=Survival of the Scheming: A Genetically Informed Link Between the Dark Triad and Mental Toughness |journal=Twin Research and Human Genetics |date=December 2013 |volume=16 |issue=6 |pages=1087–1095 |doi=10.1017/thg.2013.66 |pmid=24074275 }}</ref>

One particular study found a gene responsible for dopamine reception was positively associated with individuals who scored high on the MACH IV, but it is unclear what specific mechanisms cause this effect.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Montag |first1=Christian |last2=Hall |first2=Jeremy |last3=Plieger |first3=Thomas |last4=Felten |first4=Andrea |last5=Markett |first5=Sebastian |last6=Melchers |first6=Martin |last7=Reuter |first7=Martin |title=The DRD3 Ser9Gly polymorphism, Machiavellianism, and its link to schizotypal personality |journal=Journal of Neuroscience, Psychology, and Economics |date=March 2015 |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=48–57 |doi=10.1037/npe0000034}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Bereczkei |first1=Tamás |title=Machiavellianism: The Psychology of Manipulation |date=2017 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-351-60558-8 |page=92}}</ref> A study noted that the emotionality of Machiavellianism may also be genetically determined, with the authors stating that "it can be expected that in the case of Machiavellianism, the genetic influence may manifest itself by affecting the emotional sphere. That affective insensitivity – as McIlwain (2003) designates it--makes Machiavellians similar to psychopaths. In the study by Vernon et al (2008), genetic factors for Machiavellianism and psychopathy were correlated, which suggests that the variability of both qualities is greatly affected by the same genes. The genetically determined "cool syndrome" makes it easier for the child to use effective manipulation, leading to the development of a permanent behaviour strategy, at the same time protecting the child from internal punishments such as shame or guilt."<ref name="Siwy-Hudowska-2014">{{cite journal |first1=Anna |last1=Siwy-Hudowska |first2=Irena |last2=Pilch |date=2014 |title=Machiavellianism in families: analysis of relationships between the machaiavellanism level of grown-up children and their parents |journal=Studia Psychologiczne |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=16–23}}</ref>

Studies have found a link between Machiavellianism and a blunted [[cortisol awaking response]] (CAR).<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Megan M. |last2=Caron |first2=Kelly M. |last3=Mikolajewski |first3=Amy J. |last4=Shirtcliff |first4=Elizabeth A. |last5=Eckel |first5=Lisa A. |last6=Taylor |first6=Jeanette |title=Psychopathic Traits, Empathy, and Aggression are Differentially Related to Cortisol Awakening Response |journal=Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment |date=September 2014 |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=380–388 |doi=10.1007/s10862-014-9412-7}}</ref> A person's cortisol awaking response has been associated with a lack of affective empathy, and is highly heritable.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bartels |first1=Meike |last2=De Geus |first2=Eco J. C. |last3=Kirschbaum |first3=Clemens |last4=Sluyter |first4=Frans |last5=Boomsma |first5=Dorret I. |title=Heritability of Daytime Cortisol Levels in Children |journal=Behavior Genetics |date=2003 |volume=33 |issue=4 |pages=421–433 |doi=10.1023/A:1025321609994 |pmid=14574141 |hdl=1871/18129 |url=https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/3c17c6f3-1f86-4440-9136-035f699747bc|hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wüst |first1=Stefan |last2=Federenko |first2=Ilona |last3=Hellhammer |first3=Dirk H |last4=Kirschbaum |first4=C |title=Genetic factors, perceived chronic stress, and the free cortisol response to awakening |journal=Psychoneuroendocrinology |date=October 2000 |volume=25 |issue=7 |pages=707–720 |doi=10.1016/S0306-4530(00)00021-4 |pmid=10938450}}</ref>

'''Environmental causes'''

The environmental causes (such as shared, and non-shared environment) that contribute to the development of machiavellianism were childhood maltreatment and neglect, social reinforcement of manipulative behaviors from an early age, and poor family functioning.<ref name="Monaghan-2018"/><ref name="Lang-2015">{{cite journal |last1=Láng |first1=András |last2=Lénárd |first2=Kata |title=The relation between memories of childhood psychological maltreatment and Machiavellianism |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=April 2015 |volume=77 |pages=81–85 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2014.12.054}}</ref> One study even stated that "the etiology of Machiavellianism, similarly to the development of a dismissing-avoidant pattern, partly originates from childhood experiences obtained in relationships with unexpressive, less understanding, highly punitive or restrictive caregivers".<ref>This claim was made by <br />
*{{cite journal |last1=Ináncsi |first1=Tamás |last2=Láng |first2=András |last3=Bereczkei |first3=Tamás |title=Machiavellianism and Adult Attachment in General Interpersonal Relationships and Close Relationships |journal=Europe's Journal of Psychology |date=27 February 2015 |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=139–154 |doi=10.5964/ejop.v11i1.801 |pmid=27247647 |pmc=4873099}} <br />–and repeated by:
* {{cite journal |last1=Jonason |first1=Peter K. |last2=Lyons |first2=Minna |last3=Bethell |first3=Emily |title=The making of Darth Vader: Parent–child care and the Dark Triad |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=September 2014 |volume=67 |pages=30–34 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2013.10.006}}
* {{cite journal |last1=Láng |first1=András |last2=Birkás |first2=Béla |title=Machiavellianism and perceived family functioning in adolescence |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=June 2014 |volume=63 |pages=69–74 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2014.01.065}}</ref> In many studies, Machiavellianism has been heavily correlated with negative home atmospheres, loneliness, and adverse parental experiences. One study noted that punishment specifically led to the "emergence of deceitful and exploitative interpersonal tactics." The authors of the study concluded that these results "might give further support for the idea that Machiavellian personality traits are possible strategic responses to childhood adversities".<ref name="Lang-2015"/> Another study found the traits of Machiavellianism to be a response to early [[List of maladaptive schemas|maladaptive schemas]] (EMS), essentially coping mechanisms for emotional deprivation, mistrust, abuse, and caregiver rejection.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Láng |first1=András |title=Machiavellianism and early maladaptive schemas in adolescents |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=December 2015 |volume=87 |pages=162–165 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2015.07.039}}</ref> Irregular parent care, such as a mother being neglectful and a father being overprotective, has also been correlated with Machiavellianism.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abell |first1=Loren |last2=Lyons |first2=Minna |last3=Brewer |first3=Gayle |title=The relationship between parental bonding, Machiavellianism and adult friendship quality |journal=Individual Differences Research |date=2014 |volume=12 |issue=4–B |pages=191–197 |doi=10.65030/idr.12018 }}</ref> The hereditary influence on Machiavellianism may make it challenging to disentangle the genetic underpinnings from the effects of parental upbringing and environmental factors.<ref name="Massey-Abernathy-2016">{{cite journal |last1=Massey-Abernathy |first1=Amber |last2=Byrd-Craven |first2=Jennifer |title=Seeing but Not Feeling: Machiavellian Traits in Relation to Physiological Empathetic Responding and Life Experiences |journal=Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology |date=September 2016 |volume=2 |issue=3 |pages=252–266 |doi=10.1007/s40750-016-0041-0}}</ref> Another study also echoed similarly that it is difficult to separate genetic contributions from parenting environments, and that  "negative fathers might be high on Machiavellian traits and therefore, the transmission might be genetic rather than experiential".<ref name="Massey-Abernathy-2016"/>

In general, Jones (2020) asserts that "there may be a myriad of reasons, including some environmental reasons, as to why someone would become cynical, habitually ignore morality, or use manipulative persuasion. There may be others who are born cynical, manipulative, and amoral. Thus, there may be differences in etiology that lead to differences in how fixed the trait is, and how it is expressed".<ref name="Jones2020"/>

===Machiavellianism in children===
Ever since the creation of the construct in the 1960s, there has been extensive research on Machiavellianism in young children and adolescents, via a measure dubbed the "Kiddie Mach" test.{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=331}}<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chabrol |first1=Henri |last2=Van Leeuwen |first2=Nikki |last3=Rodgers |first3=Rachel |last4=Séjourné |first4=Natalène |title=Contributions of psychopathic, narcissistic, Machiavellian, and sadistic personality traits to juvenile delinquency |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=November 2009 |volume=47 |issue=7 |pages=734–739 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2009.06.020}}</ref> The first study was done in 1966 as a part of Dorothea Braginsky's doctoral dissertation, with the subjects being as young as 10 years old.{{sfn|Christie|Geis|1970|p=331}} Studies have shown that traits of Machiavellianism and other dark triad traits were already present in preschool children,<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1037/12352-010 |chapter=Early adoption of Machiavellian attitudes: Implications for children's interpersonal relationships |title=Narcissism and Machiavellianism in youth: Implications for the development of adaptive and maladaptive behavior |date=2011 |last1=Slaughter |first1=Virginia |pages=177–192 |isbn=978-1-4338-0845-6 }}</ref> and more pronounced in adolescents aged 11–17.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lau |first1=Katherine S. L. |last2=Marsee |first2=Monica A. |title=Exploring Narcissism, Psychopathy, and Machiavellianism in Youth: Examination of Associations with Antisocial Behavior and Aggression |journal=Journal of Child and Family Studies |date=April 2013 |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=355–367 |doi=10.1007/s10826-012-9586-0}}</ref> There have been studies to measure Machiavellianism in 6 year olds using adult informants to analyze the child's behavior.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Repacholi |first1=B. |last2=Slaughter |first2=V. |last3=Pritchard |first3=M. |last4=Gibbs |first4=V. |year=2004 |chapter=Theory of mind, Machiavellianism, and social functioning in childhood |title=Individual differences in theory of mind |pages=68–98 |publisher=Psychology Press |isbn=978-0-203-48850-8 }}</ref><ref name="Mealey-2003"/>  [[Child lying|Deceptive behaviors by children]] even as young as 3 were also investigated heavily.<ref>
* {{cite journal |last1=Gongola |first1=Jennifer |last2=Scurich |first2=Nicholas |last3=Quas |first3=Jodi A. |title=Detecting deception in children: A meta-analysis |journal=Law and Human Behavior |date=2017 |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=44–54 |doi=10.1037/lhb0000211 |pmid=27685642 |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0pw2b0fc}}
* {{Cite journal |last=Lee |first=Kang |date=June 2013 |title=Little Liars: Development of Verbal Deception in Children |journal=Child Development Perspectives |language=en |volume=7 |issue=2 |pages=91–96 |doi=10.1111/cdep.12023 |pmc=3653594 |pmid=23687515}} 
* {{Cite book |last1=Mitchell |first1=Robert W. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AeuNBW46P8AC&dq=deception+in+children&pg=PA271 |title=Deception: Perspectives on Human and Nonhuman Deceit |last2=Thompson |first2=Nicholas S. |date=1986-01-01 |publisher=State University of New York Press |isbn=978-1-4384-1332-7 |language=en}}</ref>  Peer reports suggest that children higher in Machiavellianism exhibit behaviors such as using both prosocial and coercive approaches based on how much is to be gained in a situation, and they tend to manipulate indirectly.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abell |first1=Loren |last2=Qualter |first2=Pamela |last3=Brewer |first3=Gayle |last4=Barlow |first4=Alexandra |last5=Stylianou |first5=Maria |last6=Henzi |first6=Peter |last7=Barrett |first7=Louise |title=Why Machiavellianism Matters in Childhood: The Relationship Between Children's Machiavellian Traits and Their Peer Interactions in a Natural Setting |journal=Europe's Journal of Psychology |date=20 August 2015 |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=484–493 |doi=10.5964/ejop.v11i3.957 |pmc=4873058 |pmid=27247672}}</ref> Children who score highly on the Machiavellianism scale tend to be more successful in manipulation, do it more frequently, and are judged as better at manipulation than those who score lower.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Braginsky |first1=Dorothea D. |title=Machiavellianism and manipulative interpersonal behavior in children |journal=Journal of Experimental Social Psychology |date=January 1970 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=77–99 |doi=10.1016/0022-1031(70)90077-6}}</ref> Parental levels of Machiavellianism seem to have a slight effect on the child's own level. Machiavellianism levels in fathers was positively correlated with the Machiavellianism levels of their children, but the mother's level had no significant effect. One study concluded that "parental Machiavellianism is a predictor and perhaps a cause of children's Machiavellian beliefs and their manipulative success".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kraut |first1=Robert E. |last2=Price |first2=J. Douglas |title=Machiavellianism in parents and their children |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |date=1976 |volume=33 |issue=6 |pages=782–786 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.33.6.782 |pmid=1271237}}</ref> Machiavellianism is also correlated with childhood aggression, especially concerning the control of social hierarchies.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kerig |first1=Patricia K. |last2=Stellwagen |first2=Kurt K. |title=Roles of Callous-Unemotional Traits, Narcissism, and Machiavellianism in Childhood Aggression |journal=Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment |date=September 2010 |volume=32 |issue=3 |pages=343–352 |doi=10.1007/s10862-009-9168-7}}</ref> One study found a trend upwards with respect to Machiavellianism from late childhood to adolescence, when levels of Machiavellianism are thought to peak. From adolescence throughout adulthood there is a significant and steady downward trend with regard to levels of Machiavellianism, until the age of 65 where an overall lifetime minimum is reached.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Götz |first1=Friedrich M. |last2=Bleidorn |first2=Wiebke |last3=Rentfrow |first3=Peter J. |title=Age differences in Machiavellianism across the life span: Evidence from a large-scale cross-sectional study |journal=Journal of Personality |date=October 2020 |volume=88 |issue=5 |pages=978–992 |doi=10.1111/jopy.12545 |pmid=32145085}}</ref>

Peer ratings of children high on Machiavellianism are inconsistent, with some researchers reporting that juvenile High Machs are rated as popular,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hawley |first1=Patricia H. |title=Prosocial and Coercive Configurations of Resource Control in Early Adolescence: A Case for the Well-Adapted Machiavellian |journal=Merrill-Palmer Quarterly |date=2003 |volume=49 |issue=3 |pages=279–309 |doi=10.1353/mpq.2003.0013 |hdl=1808/15796 |hdl-access=free}}</ref> and some reporting that they are less well liked by peers.<ref>{{cite thesis |last1=Palmen |first1=J. M. H. |title=Friendship and Aggression in Elementary School. The friendships of aggressive children and the effects of having aggressive friends |date=15 June 2009 |hdl=1874/34096}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Abell |first1=Loren |last2=Qualter |first2=Pamela |last3=Brewer |first3=Gayle |last4=Barlow |first4=Alexandra |last5=Stylianou |first5=Maria |last6=Henzi |first6=Peter |last7=Barrett |first7=Louise |title=Why Machiavellianism Matters in Childhood: The Relationship Between Children's Machiavellian Traits and Their Peer Interactions in a Natural Setting |journal=Europe's Journal of Psychology |date=20 August 2015 |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=484–493 |doi=10.5964/ejop.v11i3.957 |pmid=27247672 |pmc=4873058}}</ref> A study involving Greek children ages 8–12 noted that the children highest in Machiavellianism showed aggressive tendencies and were more likely to bully others, though the tactics varied by gender.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Andreou |first=Eleni |title=Bully/victim problems and their association with psychological constructs in 8- to 12-year-old Greek schoolchildren |journal=Aggressive Behavior |volume=26 |issue=1 |date=2000 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1098-2337(2000)26:1<49::AID-AB4>3.0.CO;2-M |pages=49–56}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Andreou |first=Eleni |title=Bully/victim problems and their association with Machiavellianism and self-efficacy in Greek primary school children |journal=British Journal of Educational Psychology |volume=74 |issue=2 |date=2004 |doi=10.1348/000709904773839897 |pages=297–309 |pmid=15130193}}</ref>

== Dark triad==
{{Main|Dark triad}}
In 1998, John McHoskey, William Worzel, and Christopher Szyarto proposed that narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy are more or less interchangeable in normal samples.<ref name="McHoskey-1995">{{cite journal |last1=McHoskey |first1=John |title=Narcissism and Machiavellianism |journal=Psychological Reports |date=December 1995 |volume=77 |issue=3 |pages=755–759 |doi=10.2466/pr0.1995.77.3.755 |pmid=8559913}}</ref>{{sfn|McHoskey|Worzel|Szyarto|1998}} [[Delroy L. Paulhus]] and McHoskey debated these perspectives at an [[American Psychological Association]] conference, inspiring a body of research that continues to grow in the published literature. Delroy Paulhus and Kevin Williams found enough differences between the traits to suggest that they were distinct despite their similarities, thus the concept of a "triad" of offensive personality traits was conceptualized.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://blogs.scientificamerican.com/beautiful-minds/the-light-triad-vs-dark-triad-of-personality/ |title=The Light Triad vs. Dark Triad of Personality}}</ref> There has been research on Machiavellianism using various dark triad measures, including the ''Short Dark Triad'' (SD3), and the ''[[Dark Triad Dirty Dozen]]'' test.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jonason |first1=Peter K. |last2=Webster |first2=Gregory D. |title=The dirty dozen: A concise measure of the dark triad |journal=Psychological Assessment |date=June 2010 |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=420–432 |doi=10.1037/a0019265 |pmid=20528068}}</ref><ref name="Jones-2014">{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Daniel N. |last2=Paulhus |first2=Delroy L. |title=Introducing the Short Dark Triad (SD3): A Brief Measure of Dark Personality Traits |journal=Assessment |date=February 2014 |volume=21 |issue=1 |pages=28–41 |doi=10.1177/1073191113514105 |pmid=24322012}}</ref>

Miller, Lynam, and Sharpe (2022) state that the reason why the multidimensional nature of Machiavellianism has "received less attention" is because there is "little research on Machiavellianism outside the context of the D3".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=Joshua D |last2=Sharpe |first2=Brinkley M |last3=Lynam |first3=Donald R |chapter=Controversies surrounding the Dark Triad: A call to action |pages=284–293 |chapter-url={{GBurl|eKSbEAAAQBAJ|p=284}} |editor1-last=Jonason |editor1-first=Peter Karl |title=Shining Light on the Dark Side of Personality: Measurement Properties and Theoretical Advances |date=2022 |publisher=Hogrefe Publishing GmbH |isbn=978-1-61676-615-3 }}</ref>

===Psychopathy===
Many psychologists consider Machiavellianism to be essentially indistinguishable from psychopathy, as they both share manipulative tendencies, disregard for morality, and cold callousness as their primary attributes.<ref>As this is a recurring theme in the Machiavellianism literature, this list is by no means exhaustive:

</ref><ref name="Lee-2005">{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Kibeom |last2=Ashton |first2=Michael C. |title=Psychopathy, Machiavellianism, and Narcissism in the Five-Factor Model and the HEXACO model of personality structure |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=May 2005 |volume=38 |issue=7 |pages=1571–1582 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2004.09.016}}</ref> There is an immense and ongoing debate amongst researchers as to whether or not Machiavellianism and psychopathy should be treated as the same construct, or at least treat Machiavellianism as a subset of psychopathy.<ref>

* {{harvnb|Muris|Merckelbach|Otgaar|Meijer|2017|p=188}}
</ref> When tested, High Machs scored consistently high on measures of psychopathy, more than Low Machs. Primary psychopaths also scored higher on the Machiavellianism scale than secondary psychopaths.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Skinner |first1=Nicholas F. |title=Personality correlates of Machiavellianism: VI. Machiavellianism and the psychopath |journal=Social Behavior and Personality|date=1988 |volume=16 |issue=1 |pages=33–37 |doi=10.2224/sbp.1988.16.1.33|doi-access=free }}</ref> According to John McHoskey, the MACH-IV test is merely "a global measure of psychopathy in noninstitutionalized populations", and that this is a result of the disconnect between clinical and personality psychology.{{sfn|McHoskey|Worzel|Szyarto|1998}} Many have stated that the Machiavellianism scale measures nothing more than  "successful" psychopathy, or psychopathy without the extreme clinical characteristics.<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1037/12352-002 |chapter=Psychopathy, narcissism, and Machiavellianism: Distinct yet intertwining personality constructs |title=Narcissism and Machiavellianism in youth: Implications for the development of adaptive and maladaptive behavior |date=2011 |pages=25–45 |isbn=978-1-4338-0845-6 |editor-last1=Stellwagen |editor-first1=Kurt K. |last1=Stellwagen |first1=Kurt K. |publisher=American Psychological Association |location=Washington }}</ref> Even compared to other "dark" traits, research has shown that Psychopathy correlates with Machiavellianism far more than it correlates with narcissism.<ref name="Lee-2005"/>{{sfn|Lyons|2019|p=4}} Some authors have stated that Machiavellianism and psychopathy represent the issue of a [[Jingle-jangle fallacies|jangle fallacy]], as both constructs are named differently yet describe the same concept.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kowalski |first1=Christopher Marcin |last2=Vernon |first2=Philip A. |last3=Schermer |first3=Julie Aitken |title=The Dark Triad and facets of personality |journal=Current Psychology |volume=40 |issue=11 |date=2021 |doi=10.1007/s12144-019-00518-0 |pages=5547–5558}}</ref> A 2022 paper stated that Machiavellianism "is theoretically distinct from psychopathy, but empirically they are nearly indistinguishable".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kay |first1=Cameron S. |last2=Arrow |first2=Holly |title=Taking an elemental approach to the conceptualization and measurement of Machiavellianism, narcissism, and psychopathy |journal=Social and Personality Psychology Compass |volume=16 |issue=4 |date=2022 |doi=10.1111/spc3.12662 |article-number=e12662 }}</ref> Beverly Fehr even suggested that psychopaths may be simply "High Machs who have had run up against the law".<ref name="Fehr-2013"/> [[Robert D. Hare|Robert Hare]], author of the Psychopathy Checklist, stated that Machiavellianism is more closely related to PCL Factor 1, affective detachment, than to Factor 2, an antisocial lifestyle.<ref name="Loftus"/> According to [[Christopher Patrick]], high Psychopathy Checklist scores correlated with much higher Machiavellianism scores, as well as higher scores on boldness and aggressiveness.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Patrick |first1=Christopher J. |last2=Fowles |first2=Don C. |last3=Krueger |first3=Robert F. |title=Triarchic conceptualization of psychopathy: Developmental origins of disinhibition, boldness, and meanness |journal=Development and Psychopathology |date=August 2009 |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=913–938 |doi=10.1017/S0954579409000492 |pmid=19583890 }}</ref>

Researchers note that Machiavellianism is well represented in every measure of psychopathy, such as the Factor 1 characteristics on the [[Psychopathy Checklist]], more specifically traits such as "conning/manipulative", "[[pathological lying]]," "callous/lack of empathy", and "glibness/superficial charm".<ref name="Miller-2017">{{cite journal |last1=Miller |first1=Joshua D. |last2=Hyatt |first2=Courtland S. |last3=Maples-Keller |first3=Jessica L. |last4=Carter |first4=Nathan T. |last5=Lynam |first5=Donald R. |title=Psychopathy and Machiavellianism: A Distinction Without a Difference? |journal=Journal of Personality |date=August 2017 |volume=85 |issue=4 |pages=439–453 |doi=10.1111/jopy.12251 |pmid=26971566}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Glenn|Sellbom|2015}}</ref><ref>
* {{cite book |first1=Doris |last1=McIlwain |first2=Jess |last2=Evans |first3=Eleni |last3=Caldis |first4=Fred |last4=Cicchini |first5=Avi |last5=Aronstan |first6=Adam |last6=Wright |first7=Alan |last7=Taylor |chapter=Strange Moralities: Vicarious Emotion and Moral Emotions in Machiavellian and Psychopathic Personality Styles |pages=119–148 |editor-last1=Langdon |editor-last2=MacKenzie |editor-first1=Robyn |editor-first2=Catriona |title=Emotions, Imagination, and Moral Reasoning |date=2012 |isbn=978-1-136-63165-8 |doi=10.4324/9780203803134}}
* {{cite journal |last1=Skeem |first1=Jennifer L. |last2=Polaschek |first2=Devon L. L. |last3=Patrick |first3=Christopher J. |last4=Lilienfeld |first4=Scott O. |title=Psychopathic Personality: Bridging the Gap Between Scientific Evidence and Public Policy |journal=Psychological Science in the Public Interest |date=December 2011 |volume=12 |issue=3 |pages=95–162 |doi=10.1177/1529100611426706 |pmid=26167886}}</ref><ref name="Fehr-2013"/> Donald Lynam and others noted that Machiavellianism is also represented in the "Interpersonal Manipulation" factor in Hare's Self-Report Psychopathy Scale-III and in the "Manipulation" scale in the Elemental Psychopathy Assessment. The researchers state that "ultimately, measures of psychopathy and MACH appear to be measuring the same construct, and MACH assessments fail to capture the construct as articulated in theoretical descriptions".<ref name="Miller-2017"/> Michael Levenson, author of the [[Levenson Self-Report Psychopathy Scale]], disagreed with the notion of distinguishing machiavellianism from psychopathy, stating that it "does not accord" with empirical research which shows Machiavellianism being heavily related to primary psychopathy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Levenson |first1=Michael R. |title=Psychopaths are Not Necessarily Impulsive, etc.: A Reply to Feelgood and Rantzen |journal=Theory & Psychology |date=May 1993 |volume=3 |issue=2 |pages=229–234 |doi=10.1177/0959354393032007}}</ref> Machiavellianism has a strong relationship with both primary and secondary psychopathy on Levenson's self report test.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lilienfeld |first1=Scott O |title=Methodological advances and developments in the assessment of psychopathy |journal=Behaviour Research and Therapy |date=January 1998 |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=99–125 |doi=10.1016/S0005-7967(97)10021-3 |pmid=9613020 }}</ref> In experiments High Machs also scored highly on the Psychopathic Deviate subscale on the [[MMPI]].<ref name="Mealey-2003">{{cite book |last1=Mealey |first1=Linda |last2=Kinner |first2=Stuart |title=The Social Brain |chapter=Psychopathy, Machiavellianism and Theory of Mind |publisher=Wiley |date=2003-03-14 |isbn=978-0-470-84960-6 |doi=10.1002/0470867221.ch16 |pages=355–372}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ray |first1=J. J. |last2=Ray |first2=J. A. B. |title=Some Apparent Advantages of Subclinical Psychopathy |journal=The Journal of Social Psychology |volume=117 |issue=1 |date=1982 |doi=10.1080/00224545.1982.9713415 |pages=135–142 |pmid=7109561}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Skinner |first1=Nicholas F. |title=Personality Correlates of Machiavellianism: IV. Machiavellianism and Psychopathology |journal=Social Behavior and Personality |date=1982 |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=201–203 |doi=10.2224/sbp.1982.10.2.201 |doi-access=free }}</ref> On the [[Psychopathic Personality Inventory]], created by [[Scott Lilienfeld]] and Brian Andrews, there is even a subscale similarly named [[Psychopathic Personality Inventory#Original subscales|"Machiavellian Egocentricity"]].<ref>
* {{cite journal |last1=Lilienfeld |first1=Scott O. |last2=Andrews |first2=Brian P. |title=Development and Preliminary Validation of a Self-Report Measure of Psychopathic Personality Traits in Noncriminal Population |journal=Journal of Personality Assessment |volume=66 |issue=3 |date=1996 |doi=10.1207/s15327752jpa6603_3 |pages=488–524 |pmid=8667144 |quote=Factor 1, Machiavellian Egocentricity, contains elements of Christie and Geis' (1969) Machiavellianism construct and appears similar to the construct of 'Ruthless Practicality' identified by Hundleby and Ross (1977) in their factor analysis of psychopathy-related measures.}}
* {{cite journal |last1=Kastner |first1=Rebecca M. |last2=Sellbom |first2=Martin |last3=Lilienfeld |first3=Scott O. |title=A comparison of the psychometric properties of the psychopathic personality inventory full-length and short-form versions |journal=Psychological Assessment |date=March 2012 |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=261–267 |doi=10.1037/a0025832 |pmid=22004537}}
* {{cite journal |last1=Benning |first1=Stephen D. |last2=Patrick |first2=Christopher J. |last3=Hicks |first3=Brian M. |last4=Blonigen |first4=Daniel M. |last5=Krueger |first5=Robert F. |title=Factor Structure of the Psychopathic Personality Inventory: Validity and Implications for Clinical Assessment |journal=Psychological Assessment |date=2003 |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=340–350 |doi=10.1037/1040-3590.15.3.340 |pmid=14593834}}
</ref><ref name="Poythress-1998">{{cite journal |last1=Poythress |first1=Norman G. |last2=Edens |first2=John F. |last3=Lilienfeld |first3=Scott O. |title=Criterion-related validity of the Psychopathic Personality Inventory in a prison sample |journal=Psychological Assessment |date=December 1998 |volume=10 |issue=4 |pages=426–430 |doi=10.1037/1040-3590.10.4.426}}</ref> The subscale is said to assess a "ruthless and self centered willingness to exploit others".<ref name="Poythress-1998"/><ref>{{Cite book |last=Patrick |first=Christopher J. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2CmPDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA167 |title=Handbook of Psychopathy |date=2019-06-14 |publisher=Guilford Publications |isbn=978-1-4625-4123-2 |language=en}}</ref> Machiavellianism and psychopathy have both been negatively correlated with the recognition of facial emotions, with one study stating that "if the ability to recognise facial expressions is exclusively an affective empathy task, it indeed accounts for the facial recognition deficits found in primary psychopathy and Machiavellianism."<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wai |first1=Michael |last2=Tiliopoulos |first2=Niko |title=The affective and cognitive empathic nature of the dark triad of personality |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=May 2012 |volume=52 |issue=7 |pages=794–799 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2012.01.008}}</ref> High scores on the ''Triarchic Psychopathy Measure'' questionnaire (especially the "Meanness" subscale) strongly correlated with Machiavellianism.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00223891.2012.735302 | doi=10.1080/00223891.2012.735302 | title=Elaborating on the Construct Validity of the Triarchic Psychopathy Measure in a Criminal Offender Sample | date=2013 | last1=Stanley | first1=Jennifer H. | last2=Wygant | first2=Dustin B. | last3=Sellbom | first3=Martin | journal=Journal of Personality Assessment | volume=95 | issue=4 | pages=343–350 | pmid=23113864 | hdl=1885/33374 | hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Sica |first1=Claudio |last2=Drislane |first2=Laura |last3=Caudek |first3=Corrado |last4=Angrilli |first4=Alessandro |last5=Bottesi |first5=Gioia |last6=Cerea |first6=Silvia |last7=Ghisi |first7=Marta |title=A test of the construct validity of the Triarchic Psychopathy Measure in an Italian community sample |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=August 2015 |volume=82 |pages=163–168 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2015.03.015 }}</ref> One group of researchers noted that by definition, "the interpersonal features of psychopathy involve a calculating, cunning, and manipulative style" thus a highly psychopathic person is ''ipso facto'' also a person high on Machiavellianism.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=DeLisi |first1=Matt |last2=Pechorro |first2=Pedro |last3=Maroco |first3=João |last4=Simões |first4=Mário |title=Overlapping measures or constructs? An empirical study of the overlap between self-control, psychopathy, Machiavellianism and narcissism |journal=Forensic Science International: Synergy |date=2021 |volume=3 |article-number=100141 |doi=10.1016/j.fsisyn.2021.100141 |pmid=33665594 |pmc=7903057 }}</ref>

Machiavellianism and psychopathy overlap so heavily that researchers have proposed merging the two traits into each other, preferably incorporating Machiavellianism into psychopathy.<ref>{{harvnb|Glenn|Sellbom|2015}}</ref> There have been attempts to combine Machiavellianism and psychopathy into one construct, such as the creation of a "Dark Dyad" as opposed to a "Dark Triad", with the exclusion of narcissism.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rogoza |first1=Radosław |last2=Cieciuch |first2=Jan |title=Dark Triad traits and their structure: An empirical approach |journal=Current Psychology |volume=39 |issue=4 |date=2020 |doi=10.1007/s12144-018-9834-6 |pages=1287–1302|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Egan |first1=Vincent |last2=Chan |first2=Stephanie |last3=Shorter |first3=Gillian W. |title=The Dark Triad, happiness and subjective well-being |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |publisher=Elsevier BV |volume=67 |year=2014 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2014.01.004 |pages=17–22 |url=https://pure.qub.ac.uk/en/publications/3627e8c2-9f8c-4371-a517-93ce6b3ed18a }}</ref>

A 2019 study done on criminal psychopaths noted that Machiavellianism showed the strongest association with the affective aspect of psychopathy.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kavish |first1=Nicholas |last2=Jones |first2=Michelle A. |last3=Rock |first3=Rachel C. |last4=Johnson |first4=Alexandria K. |last5=Anderson |first5=Jaime L. |title=On the Overlap between Psychopathic Traits and Machiavellianism in a Forensic Population |journal=Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment |date=June 2019 |volume=41 |issue=2 |pages=198–207 |doi=10.1007/s10862-018-9708-0}}</ref>

====Difference between constructs:Impulse control====

Many other psychologists state that while Machiavellianism and psychopathy overlap heavily, there is much evidence to suggest that they are distinct personality constructs.<ref name="Jones-2009"/><ref name="Measures">{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-386915-9.00020-6 |chapter=Measures of Dark Personalities |title=Measures of Personality and Social Psychological Constructs |pages=562–594 |year=2015 |last1=Paulhus |first1=Delroy L. |last2=Jones |first2=Daniel N. |isbn=978-0-12-386915-9}}</ref><ref name="Jones-2022">{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Daniel N. |last2=Mueller |first2=Steven M. |title=Is Machiavellianism Dead or Dormant? The Perils of Researching a Secretive Construct |journal=Journal of Business Ethics |date=March 2022 |volume=176 |issue=3 |pages=535–549 |doi=10.1007/s10551-020-04708-w}}</ref> Psychologists who stress the differences between Machiavellianism and psychopathy state that, in total contrast to high Machs, psychopaths are impulsive, tend to be reckless, and lack long term planning skills.<ref name="Collison-2018"/><ref name="Paulhus-2002">{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/S0092-6566(02)00505-6 |title=The Dark Triad of personality: Narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy |journal=Journal of Research in Personality |volume=36 |issue=6 |pages=556–563 |year=2002 |last1=Paulhus |first1=Delroy L. |last2=Williams |first2=Kevin M. }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |doi=10.4324/9781315106922-4 |chapter=Dark Triad |title=Machiavellianism |date=2017 |last1=Bereczkei |first1=Tamás |pages=44–52 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-315-10692-2}}</ref> [[Delroy Paulhus]] and others have stated that this difference between the two traits is often underappreciated.<ref name="Jones-2014"/> Scholars also note that those high on Machiavellianism can delay gratification, and have more sensitivity to punishment and awareness of consequences than psychopaths.<ref name="Jones-2022"/> Though both traits have a heritable basis, Machiavellianism is more influenced by the environment than psychopathy.<ref name="Siwy-Hudowska-2014"/> High Machs have been described as "master manipulators" and far better at manipulation than psychopaths and narcissists.<ref>
* Jones, Daniel N.; Paulhus, Delroy L. (2010). "Differentiating the Dark Triad within the Interpersonal Circumplex". Handbook of Interpersonal Psychology. pp. 249–267. doi:10.1002/9781118001868.ch15. ISBN 978-0-470-47160-9.
* {{harvnb|Jones|Paulhus|2014}}
* {{cite book |last1=Bereczkei |first1=Tamás |title=Machiavellianism: The Psychology of Manipulation |date=2017 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-351-60558-8}}
* {{cite journal |last1=Sharpe |first1=Brinkley M. |last2=Collison |first2=Katherine L. |last3=Lynam |first3=Donald R. |last4=Miller |first4=Joshua D. |title=Does Machiavellianism meaningfully differ from psychopathy? It depends |journal=Behavioral Sciences & the Law |date=October 2021 |volume=39 |issue=5 |pages=663–677 |doi=10.1002/bsl.2538 |pmid=34636074 |url=https://psyarxiv.com/4r3a7/}}</ref>

Daniel Jones notes that even though both psychopaths and High Machs share a manipulative and callous nature, the difference between Machiavellianism and psychopathy lies in the type of manipulation employed by the two constructs. Machiavellianism is marked by cautious planning, and manipulating only when something is to be gained, while psychopathy is marked by rashness, and manipulating regardless of situation.<ref name="Jones2020">{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-24612-3_1245 |chapter=Machiavellianism |title=Encyclopedia of Personality and Individual Differences |date=2020 |last1=Jones |first1=Daniel N. |pages=2710–2718 |isbn=978-3-319-24610-9 }}</ref> O'Boyle and others found however that the notion that Machiavellianism is marked by cautiousness does not match empirical research which shows that it can be correlated with reckless behavior in certain situations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=O'Boyle |first1=Ernest H. |last2=Forsyth |first2=Donelson R. |last3=Banks |first3=George C. |last4=Story |first4=Paul A. |last5=White |first5=Charles D. |title=A Meta-Analytic Test of Redundancy and Relative Importance of the Dark Triad and Five-Factor Model of Personality |journal=Journal of Personality |date=December 2015 |volume=83 |issue=6 |pages=644–664 |doi=10.1111/jopy.12126 |pmid=25168647 }}</ref>

In response to this interpretation, Miller et al (2017) responded by saying that empirical research casts "substantial doubt" on the notion of Machiavellianism being distinguishable from psychopathy, and that ultimately literature on Machiavellianism should be framed as an alternative literature on psychopathy, as they view that Machiavellianism literature is far more helpful in understanding psychopathy.<ref name="Miller-2017"/>

===Narcissism===

Individuals high in Machiavellianism and narcissism both manipulate to improve their reputations, and how they appear to others.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rauthmann |first1=John F. |title=Acquisitive or protective self-presentation of dark personalities? Associations among the Dark Triad and self-monitoring |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=September 2011 |volume=51 |issue=4 |pages=502–508 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2011.05.008}}</ref><ref name="Lyons-2019">{{cite book |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-814291-2.00006-1 |chapter=The Dark Triad in the Workplace |title=The Dark Triad of Personality |date=2019b |last1=Lyons |first1=Minna |pages=137–160 |publisher=Elsevier |isbn=978-0-12-814291-2}}</ref> Individuals high in the two traits do this as a form of self aggrandizement to help their chances of success in a given situation.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tracy |first1=Jessica L. |last2=Cheng |first2=Joey T. |last3=Robins |first3=Richard W. |last4=Trzesniewski |first4=Kali H. |title=Authentic and Hubristic Pride: The Affective Core of Self-esteem and Narcissism |journal=Self and Identity |date=April 2009 |volume=8 |issue=2–3 |pages=196–213 |doi=10.1080/15298860802505053 }}</ref> Machiavellianism scores were positively associated with aspects of narcissism such as entitlement and exploitativeness, and inversely associated with adaptive narcissistic tendencies, like self-sufficiency.<ref name="McHoskey-1995"/> Studies have also shown that those higher on Machiavellianism are more realistic about their character, while narcissists are less realistic about theirs.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Paulhus |first1=Delroy L. |first2=Kevin |last2=Williams |first3=Peter |last3=Harms |title=Shedding light on the dark triad of personality: Narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy |conference=Annual meeting of the Society for Personality and Social Psychology |location=San Antonio, TX |date=2001 |url=http://www.alecomm.com/images/cwattachments/617_f3b5c3fa053622e1aba406c6dedaf0b1.pdf}}</ref> Compared to High Machs, narcissists are less malevolent and show a more socially positive personality. They also have higher levels of self-rated happiness.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Egan |first1=Vincent |last2=Chan |first2=Stephanie |last3=Shorter |first3=Gillian W. |title=The Dark Triad, happiness and subjective well-being |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=September 2014 |volume=67 |pages=17–22 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2014.01.004 |url=https://pure.qub.ac.uk/en/publications/the-dark-triad-happiness-and-subjective-wellbeing(3627e8c2-9f8c-4371-a517-93ce6b3ed18a).html}}</ref>

Machiavellianism and narcissism both share a lack of empathy and a focus on self-interest, though the two traits differ in how they manifest in people, and what their motivations are. High Machs have tendencies to be driven by personal gain, whereas narcissists are driven by a need for validation and admiration.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zitek |first1=Emily M. |last2=Jordan |first2=Alexander H. |title=Psychological Entitlement Predicts Failure to Follow Instructions |journal=Social Psychological and Personality Science |date=March 2019 |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=172–180 |doi=10.1177/1948550617729885}}</ref> Opposed to those high on narcissism, High Machs tend to have better self control, are less impulsive and are more self-serving their interpersonal interactions, while narcissists may be more impulsive and attention-seeking.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jones |first1=Daniel N. |last2=Paulhus |first2=Delroy L. |title=The role of impulsivity in the Dark Triad of personality |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |date=October 2011 |volume=51 |issue=5 |pages=679–682 |doi=10.1016/j.paid.2011.04.011}}</ref>

In terms of social relationships, High Machs are more likely to be more exploitative towards others, while narcissists may be more likely to seek out relationships that serve to bolster their [[self-esteem]] and provide them with the admiration they desire.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Czarna |first1=Anna Z. |last2=Jonason |first2=Peter K. |last3=Dufner |first3=Michael |last4=Kossowska |first4=Małgorzata |title=The Dirty Dozen Scale: Validation of a Polish Version and Extension of the Nomological Net |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |date=30 March 2016 |volume=7 |page=445 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00445 |doi-access=free |pmid=27065915 |pmc=4811972}}</ref>

Compared to subclinical narcissists, High Machs exhibit a greater lack of empathy, because of the emotional deficiencies inherent within Machiavellianism.<ref name="Jonason1"/>

===White collar crime===

Research has shown that individuals high in Machiavellianism may be more willing to engage in [[White-collar crime|white collar crimes]].<ref>
* {{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KPKxDQAAQBAJ&dq=maria%20konnikova&pg=PA24 |title=The Confidence Game: Why We Fall for It . . . Every Time |isbn=978-0-14-310987-7 |last1=Konnikova |first1=Maria |date=10 January 2017 |publisher=Penguin}}
* {{cite journal |last1=Li-Ping Tang |first1=Thomas |last2=Chen |first2=Yuh-Jia |last3=Sutarso |first3=Toto |title=Bad apples in bad (business) barrels: The love of money, machiavellianism, risk tolerance, and unethical behavior |journal=Management Decision |date=7 March 2008 |volume=46 |issue=2 |pages=243–263 |doi=10.1108/00251740810854140}}
* {{cite journal |last1=Utami |first1=Intiyas |last2=Wijono |first2=Sutarto |last3=Noviyanti |first3=Suzy |last4=Mohamed |first4=Nafsiah |title=Fraud diamond, Machiavellianism and fraud intention |journal=International Journal of Ethics and Systems |date=11 November 2019 |volume=35 |issue=4 |pages=531–544 |doi=10.1108/IJOES-02-2019-0042}}</ref> Psychologist Daniel Jones has stated that "individuals higher on Machiavellianism are well suited for crimes in the financial world, especially crimes that skirt the legal system".<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1037/14854-005 |chapter=The nature of Machiavellianism: Distinct patterns of misbehavior |title=The dark side of personality: Science and practice in social, personality, and clinical psychology |date=2016 |last1=Jones |first1=Daniel N. |pages=87–107 |publisher=American Psychological Association |location=Washington |isbn=978-1-4338-2187-5}}</ref> Delroy Paulhus has stated that Machiavellianism is the main trait for white collar criminals and con artists, and not psychopathy, stating that:
