{{Use dmy dates|date=November 2023}}
[[File:Stanley Kubrick in Dr. Strangelove Trailer (4) Cropped.jpg|thumb|upright=1.1|American filmmaker [[Stanley Kubrick]] was notorious for his professional perfectionism.<ref>{{cite book |last=Herr |first=Michael |title=Kubrick |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=H2DHBl6nA7cC |year=2001 |publisher=Pan Macmillan |isbn=978-0-330-48113-7 |page=56}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Ciment |first=Michel|author-link=Michel Ciment |title=Kubrick: The Definitive Edition |publisher=Faber and Faber, Inc. |year=1980 |page=38}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.visual-memory.co.uk/faq/index4.html |title=The Kubrick FAQ Part 4 |publisher=Visual-memory.co.uk |date=22 February 2002 |access-date=24 November 2011 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130524201007/http://www.visual-memory.co.uk/faq/index4.html |archive-date=24 May 2013}}</ref>]]
In [[psychology]], '''perfectionism''' is a broad [[Trait theory|personality trait]] characterized by a person's concern with striving for flawlessness and perfection and is accompanied by critical self-evaluations and concerns regarding others' evaluations.<ref name="Stoeber & Childs (2010)">{{cite journal|last=Stoeber|first=Joachim|author2=Childs, Julian H.|year=2010|title=The Assessment of Self-Oriented and Socially Prescribed Perfectionism: Subscales Make a Difference|url=http://kar.kent.ac.uk/24751/1/Stoeber%20Childs%20%282010%29%20JPA.pdf|journal=Journal of Personality Assessment|volume=92|issue=6|pages=577–585|doi=10.1080/00223891.2010.513306|pmid=20954059|s2cid=1241506|access-date=5 February 2019|archive-date=3 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103152855/https://kar.kent.ac.uk/24751/1/Stoeber%20Childs%20(2010)%20JPA.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Flett & Hewitt (2002)">{{cite book|last=Flett|first=G. L.|title=Perfectionism|author2=Hewitt, P. L.|publisher=American Psychological Association|year=2002|location=Washington, DC|pages=5–31}}</ref> It is best conceptualized as a multidimensional and multilayered personality characteristic, and initially some psychologists thought that there were many positive and negative aspects.<ref name="Yang & Stoeber" />

Maladaptive perfectionism drives people to be concerned with achieving unattainable ideals or unrealistic goals that often lead to many forms of adjustment problems such as [[Depression (mood)|depression]], [[anxiety]], [[obsessive–compulsive disorder|OCD]], [[obsessive–compulsive personality disorder|OCPD]] and low [[self-esteem]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shafran |first1=Roz |last2=Mansell |first2=Warren |title=Perfectionism and psychopathology: a review of research and treatment |journal=Clinical Psychology Review |date=August 2001 |volume=21 |issue=6 |pages=879–906 |doi=10.1016/S0272-7358(00)00072-6 |pmid=11497211 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Steinert |first1=Christiane |last2=Heim |first2=Nikolas |last3=Leichsenring |first3=Falk |title=Procrastination, Perfectionism, and Other Work-Related Mental Problems: Prevalence, Types, Assessment, and Treatment—A Scoping Review |journal=Frontiers in Psychiatry |date=11 October 2021 |volume=12 |doi=10.3389/fpsyt.2021.736776 |doi-access=free |pmid=34707522 |pmc=8542725 }}</ref> In clinical settings, this kind of perfectionism is also known as '''anankastia''', especially in obsessive–compulsive or [[personality disorder]] contexts.<ref>{{Cite Merriam-Webster|anankastic|accessdate=18 April 2026}}</ref><ref>[https://icd.who.int/browse/2026-01/mms/en#848330288 6D11.4 Anankastia in personality disorder or personality difficulty] in the [[ICD-11]]</ref> These adjustment problems often lead to [[suicidal thoughts]] and tendencies and influence or invite other psychological, physical, social, and further achievement problems in children, adolescents, and adults.

Since the late 1980s, perfectionist tendencies have been on the rise among recent generations of young people attending higher education.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Curran|first1=Thomas|last2=Hill|first2=Andrew P.|date=April 2019|title=Perfectionism is increasing over time: A meta-analysis of birth cohort differences from 1989 to 2016.|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2626/1/Curran%20%26%20Hill%20%282018%29%20PB.pdf|journal=Psychological Bulletin|volume=145|issue=4|pages=410–429|doi=10.1037/bul0000138|issn=1939-1455|pmid=29283599|s2cid=814787|access-date=2 December 2019|archive-date=21 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180721152222/https://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2626/1/Curran%20%26%20Hill%20%282018%29%20PB.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Definition ==
Perfectionists strain compulsively and unceasingly toward unattainable goals.  They measure their self-worth by productivity and accomplishments to the point that some tendencies even lead to distraction from other areas of life.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Parker |first1=W. D. |last2=Adkins |first2=K. K. |year=1995 |title=Perfectionism and the gifted |journal=Roeper Review |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=173–176 |doi=10.1080/02783199509553653}}</ref> Perfectionists pressure themselves to achieve unrealistic goals that inevitably lead to disappointment. Perfectionists tend to be harsh critics of themselves, their work, and their failure to meet their own expectations.

===Perfectionary paralysis===
''Perfectionary paralysis'' refers to a specific aspect of perfectionism in which an individual abandons their work due to an overwhelming pursuit of perfection. This occurs when the desire for flawlessness reaches such an extreme level that progress becomes impossible, leading to inaction or the complete dismissal of the task at hand. The term ''perfectionary paralysis'' is derived from two related psychological phenomena: [[creative paralysis]] and [[analysis paralysis]]. Both describe similar tendencies where overthinking or an excessive need for perfection hinders productivity and thus implicitly imply the idea of perfectionary paralysis.

===Normal vs. neurotic===
In 1978, D. E. Hamachek argued for two contrasting types of perfectionism, classifying people as tending towards [[normality (behavior)|normal]] perfectionism or [[neuroticism|neurotic]] perfectionism. Normal perfectionists are more inclined to pursue perfection without compromising their self-esteem, and derive pleasure from their efforts. Neurotic perfectionists are prone to strive for unrealistic goals and feel dissatisfied when they cannot reach them. Hamachek offers several strategies that have been proven useful in helping people change from maladaptive towards healthier behavior.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | last = Hamachek
 | first = D. E.
 | title = Psychodynamics of normal and neurotic perfectionism
 | journal = Psychology: A Journal of Human Behavior
 | volume = 15
 | pages = 27–33
 | year = 1978
 | url = http://psycnet.apa.org/psycinfo/1979-08598-001
 | access-date = 21 July 2014
| archive-date = 29 May 2015
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150529053006/http://psycnet.apa.org/psycinfo/1979-08598-001
 | url-status = live
 }}</ref> Contemporary research supports the idea that these two basic aspects of perfectionist behavior, as well as other dimensions such as "nonperfectionism", can be differentiated.<ref name="Rice, Ashby, & Gilman" /> They have been labeled differently, and are sometimes referred to as positive striving and maladaptive evaluation concerns, active and passive perfectionism, positive and negative perfectionism, and adaptive and maladaptive perfectionism.<ref name="Stoeber & Otto">{{cite journal|last=Stoeber|first=Joachim|author2=Otto, Kathleen|title=Positive Conceptions of Perfectionism: Approaches, Evidence, Challenges|journal=Personality and Social Psychology Review|year=2006|volume=10|issue=4|pages=295–319|doi=10.1207/s15327957pspr1004_2|pmid=17201590|s2cid=24588701|url=http://kar.kent.ac.uk/4481/1/Stoeber_%26_Otto_PositiveConceptions_2006.pdf|access-date=5 February 2019|archive-date=21 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180721230758/https://kar.kent.ac.uk/4481/1/Stoeber_%26_Otto_PositiveConceptions_2006.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Although there is a general perfectionism that affects all realms of life, some researchers contend that levels of perfectionism are significantly different across different domains (i.e. work, academic, sport, interpersonal relationships, home life).<ref name="Yang & Stoeber" />

However, it is debated whether perfectionism can be adaptive and has positive aspects. In fact, recent research suggests that what is termed "adaptive perfectionism" is associated with suicidal thinking,<ref name="Smith 522–542">{{Cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=Martin M.|last2=Sherry|first2=Simon B.|last3=Chen|first3=Samantha|last4=Saklofske|first4=Donald H.|last5=Mushquash|first5=Christopher|last6=Flett|first6=Gordon L.|last7=Hewitt|first7=Paul L.|date=4 September 2017|title=The perniciousness of perfectionism: A meta-analytic review of the perfectionism-suicide relationship|journal=Journal of Personality|volume=86|issue=3|pages=522–542|doi=10.1111/jopy.12333|pmid=28734118|s2cid=3188058 |issn=0022-3506|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2904/1/Smith.Sherry.Chen.Saklofske.Mushquash.Flett.Hewitt%20%282017%29%20.pdf|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=7 March 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200307195114/https://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2904/1/Smith.Sherry.Chen.Saklofske.Mushquash.Flett.Hewitt%20(2017)%20.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> depression,<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=Martin M.|last2=Sherry|first2=Simon B.|last3=Rnic|first3=Katerina|last4=Saklofske|first4=Donald H.|last5=Enns|first5=Murray|last6=Gralnick|first6=Tara|date=March 2016|title=Are Perfectionism Dimensions Vulnerability Factors for Depressive Symptoms After Controlling for Neuroticism? A Meta-analysis of 10 Longitudinal Studies|journal=European Journal of Personality|volume=30|issue=2|pages=201–212|doi=10.1002/per.2053|s2cid=11756322|issn=0890-2070|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2926/1/Smith.Sherry.Rnic.Saklofske.Enns.Gralnic.2016%20%283%29.pdf|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=23 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180723024948/https://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2926/1/Smith.Sherry.Rnic.Saklofske.Enns.Gralnic.2016%20(3).pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> eating disorders,<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last1=Castro-Fornieles|first1=Josefina|last2=Gual|first2=Pilar|last3=Lahortiga|first3=Francisca|last4=Gila|first4=Araceli|last5=Casulà|first5=Vanesa|last6=Fuhrmann|first6=Cynthia|last7=Imirizaldu|first7=Milagros|last8=Saura|first8=Begoña|last9=Martínez|first9=Esteve|last10=Toro|first10=Josep|date=2007|title=Self-oriented perfectionism in eating disorders|journal=International Journal of Eating Disorders|volume=40|issue=6|pages=562–568|doi=10.1002/eat.20393|pmid=17510925|issn=0276-3478}}</ref> poor health<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Molnar|first1=Danielle S.|last2=Sadava|first2=Stan W.|last3=Flett|first3=Gordon L.|last4=Colautti|first4=Jennifer|date=July 2012|title=Perfectionism and health: A mediational analysis of the roles of stress, social support and health-related behaviours|journal=Psychology & Health|volume=27|issue=7|pages=846–864|doi=10.1080/08870446.2011.630466|pmid=22149004|s2cid=39264723|issn=0887-0446}}</ref> and early mortality.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal|last1=Fry|first1=Prem S.|last2=Debats|first2=Dominique L.|date=21 April 2009|title=Perfectionism and the Five-factor Personality Traits as Predictors of Mortality in Older Adults|journal=Journal of Health Psychology|volume=14|issue=4|pages=513–524|doi=10.1177/1359105309103571|pmid=19383652|s2cid=41736761|issn=1359-1053}}</ref> Some researchers argue that, certainly, a construct that causes people to think more about suicide, and places them at risk for depression, eating disorders, poor health, and early mortality is far from one that is adaptive. In fact, there is no empirical support for the assertion that a healthy form of perfectionism exists. Instead, what has been termed adaptive perfectionism has little relation to perfectionism and has more to do with striving for excellence.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Blasberg|first1=Jonathan S.|last2=Hewitt|first2=Paul L.|last3=Flett|first3=Gordon L.|last4=Sherry|first4=Simon B.|last5=Chen|first5=Chang|date=3 August 2016|title=The Importance of Item Wording|journal=Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment|volume=34|issue=7|pages=702–717|doi=10.1177/0734282916653701|s2cid=148169916|issn=0734-2829}}</ref><ref name=":7" /> A relentless striving for unreasonably high expectations that are rarely achieved and an avoidance of imperfection at all costs is what distinguishes perfectionism from excellencism.<ref name=":7" /> Perfectionism therefore extends beyond adaptive strivings and is not a synonym for excellence or conscientiousness. Numerous researchers advise against using the term "adaptive perfectionism" as it is inappropriate for a personality trait.<ref>{{Citation |last=Joachim |first=Stoeber |chapter=The Psychology of Perfectionism |date=22 August 2017 |title= |pages=3–17 |publisher=Routledge |doi=10.4324/9781315536255-2 |isbn=978-1-315-53625-5}}</ref>

There is some literature that supports the usage of adaptive perfectionism when used in comparison with maladaptive perfectionism. Differences were found when these two dimensions of perfectionism were paired with the Big Five personality traits. For example, adaptive perfectionism was found to predict openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion, while maladaptive perfectionism was found to predict neuroticism.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ulu|first1=Inci Pinar|last2=Tezer|first2=Esin|date=24 May 2010|title=Adaptive and Maladaptive Perfectionism, Adult Attachment, and Big Five Personality Traits|url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00223981003784032|journal=The Journal of Psychology|language=en|volume=144|issue=4|pages=327–340|doi=10.1080/00223981003784032|pmid=20617761|s2cid=7273406|issn=0022-3980|url-access=subscription|hdl=11511/56820|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

===Strivings vs. concerns===
Psychologists J. Stoeber and K. Otto suggested that perfectionism consists of two main dimensions: perfectionist strivings and perfectionist concerns. Perfectionist strivings are associated with positive aspects of perfectionism; perfectionist concerns are associated with negative aspects (see below).
* Healthy perfectionists score high in perfectionist strivings and low in perfectionist concerns.
* Unhealthy perfectionists score high in both strivings and concerns.
* Non-perfectionists show low levels of perfectionist strivings.<ref name="Stoeber & Otto" />
Prompted by earlier research providing empirical evidence that perfectionism could be associated with positive aspects (specifically perfectionist strivings),<ref>{{Cite journal
 | last1 = Frost | first1 = R. O.
 | last2 = Heimburg | first2 = R. G.
 | last3 = Holt | first3 = C. S.
 | last4 = Mattia | first4 = J. I.
 | last5 = Neubauer | first5 = A. A.
 | title = A comparison of two measures of perfectionism
 | journal = Personality and Individual Differences
 | volume = 14 | pages = 469–489
 | year = 1993
 | doi = 10.1016/0191-8869(93)90181-2
 }}</ref> they challenged the widespread belief that perfectionism is only detrimental through a non-empirical narrative review. They claimed that people with high levels of perfectionist strivings and low levels of perfectionist concerns demonstrated more [[self-esteem]], [[agreeableness]], [[academic success]] and [[social interaction]]. This type of perfectionist also showed fewer psychological and somatic issues typically associated with perfectionism, namely [[Depression (mood)|depression]], [[anxiety]] and [[Coping (psychology)#Negative techniques (maladaptive coping or non-coping)|maladaptive coping styles]].<ref name="Stoeber & Otto" /> However, empirical meta-analytic reviews have failed to replicate these claims.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Limburg|first1=Karina|last2=Watson|first2=Hunna J.|last3=Hagger|first3=Martin S.|last4=Egan|first4=Sarah J.|date=27 December 2016|title=The Relationship Between Perfectionism and Psychopathology: A Meta-Analysis|journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology|volume=73|issue=10|pages=1301–1326|doi=10.1002/jclp.22435|pmid=28026869|hdl=20.500.11937/38934|issn=0021-9762|hdl-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=Martin M.|last2=Vidovic|first2=Vanja|last3=Sherry|first3=Simon B.|last4=Stewart|first4=Sherry H.|last5=Saklofske|first5=Donald H.|date=5 October 2017|title=Are perfectionism dimensions risk factors for anxiety symptoms? A meta-analysis of 11 longitudinal studies|journal=Anxiety, Stress, & Coping|volume=31|issue=1|pages=4–20|doi=10.1080/10615806.2017.1384466|pmid=28980487|s2cid=205726845|issn=1061-5806|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2903/1/Smith.Vidovic.Sherry.Stewart.Saklofske%20%282017%29.pdf|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=29 April 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190429092837/https://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2903/1/Smith.Vidovic.Sherry.Stewart.Saklofske%20(2017).pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kehayes|first1=Ivy-Lee L.|last2=Smith|first2=Martin M.|last3=Sherry|first3=Simon B.|last4=Vidovic|first4=Vanja|last5=Saklofske|first5=Donald H.|date=February 2019|title=Are perfectionism dimensions risk factors for bulimic symptoms? A meta-analysis of longitudinal studies|journal=Personality and Individual Differences|volume=138|pages=117–125|doi=10.1016/j.paid.2018.09.022|s2cid=149484245 |issn=0191-8869|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/3447/1/DONE%20MA%20ED%20Sep16.pdf}}</ref><ref name=":6"/><ref name="Smith 522–542" />

=== The Comprehensive Model of Perfectionist Behaviour ===
The Comprehensive Model of Perfectionism (CMPB) operationalizes perfectionism as a multilevel and multidimensional personality style that contains a trait level, a self-presentational level, and a cognitive level.

The stable, dispositional, trait-like level of this model includes self-oriented perfectionism and socially prescribed perfectionism, as well as other-oriented perfectionism.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last1=Hewitt|first1=P. L.|title=Perfectionism: A relational approach to conceptualization, assessment, and treatment. Guilford Publications.|last2=Flett|first2=G. L.|last3=Mikail|first3=S. F.|publisher=Guilford Publications|year=2017}}</ref> Self-oriented perfectionism is characterized by requiring perfection from oneself, while socially prescribed perfectionism refers to the need to obtain acceptance by fulfilling actual or perceived expectations imposed by others. In contrast, other-oriented perfectionists direct their perfectionism towards external sources and are preoccupied with expecting perfection from others.

The second component of the Comprehensive Model of Perfectionism contains the interpersonal expression of perfection through [[impression management]] and [[self-monitoring]].<ref name=":1" /> This relational component reflects the need to appear, rather than be, perfect via the promotion of perfection and the concealment of imperfection. Like the perfectionism traits, these components are also multifaceted. One of its facets, perfectionist self-promotion, refers to the expression of perfectionism by actively presenting a flawless, though often false, image of oneself.<ref name=":1" /> Another interpersonal facet, nondisplay of imperfection, is the expression of perfectionism through concealment of attributes or behaviours that may be deemed as imperfect, such as making mistakes in front of others.<ref name=":1" /> Similarly, nondisclosure of imperfection is also associated with concealment of self-aspects, but focuses on avoiding verbal disclosure of imperfections, such as not revealing personal information that may be judged negatively or admitting failures.<ref name=":1" /> All three facets are used as an (alleged) protection from feelings of low self-worth and possible rejection.

The self-relational/intrapersonal component of the CMPB refers to ruminative, perfectionist thinking and is characterized by cognitive processes concerning the need for perfection, as well as self-recriminations and a focus on the discrepancy between one's actual and ideal self. This component therefore entails the information processing related to perfectionism.<ref name=":1" /> These three components of the Comprehensive Model of Perfectionism are independent but interrelated, and can be present in individuals in heterogeneous, idiosyncratic patterns with different combinations.<ref name=":1" />

=== The Perfectionism Social Disconnection Model ===
The Perfectionism Social Disconnection Model (PSDM) is a dynamic-relational model describing perfectionism and its consequences in an interpersonal context.<ref name=":1" /> This model asserts that perfectionism, via an interpersonal style characterized by aloofness and inauthenticity, leads to the social disconnection and rejection perfectionists aim to avoid.<ref name=":11">{{Citation|last1=Hewitt|first1=Paul L.|chapter=Perfectionism in the Therapeutic Context|date=22 August 2017|title=The Psychology of Perfectionism|pages=306–330|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-315-53625-5|last2=Flett|first2=Gordon L.|last3=Mikail|first3=Samuel F.|last4=Kealy|first4=David|last5=Zhang|first5=Lisa C.|doi=10.4324/9781315536255-20}}</ref> According to the PSDM, perfectionism develops in an early interpersonal context through asynchrony between child and caregiver, when there is a lack of attunement ("fit") between the temperament of the child and caregiver responses, leading to unfulfilled needs for belonging, acceptance, and self-esteem.<ref name=":1" /> This creates a relational schema of others as critical, and rejecting, and an internal model of oneself as defective which makes perfectionists highly sensitive to the potential for judgment and rejection in interpersonal encounters.<ref name=":1" /> Consequently, according to the PSDM, perfectionism serves an interpersonal purpose and the person relies on it as a means of fulfilling the needs for belonging and self-esteem.<ref name=":1" /> In an attempt to gain a sense of acceptance and connection while avoiding possible judgment and rejection, these individuals aim to be or appear flawless. Paradoxically, this often rigid, aloof, and self-concealing relational style increases the potential for alienation and rejection and can lead to social disconnection.<ref name=":11"/> In this way, the very behaviours that perfectionists consider as purportedly fulfilling unmet relational needs exert a detrimental influence on interpersonal encounters, so the alleged solution to social disconnection actually generates it.<ref name=":11"/>                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             The PSDM also provides a link between perfectionism and its maladaptive consequences since the estrangement from oneself and others generated by perfectionism is associated with a number of adverse outcomes, such as interpersonal difficulties, depression, and suicide risk.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal|last1=Flett|first1=Gordon L.|last2=Hewitt|first2=Paul L.|last3=Heisel|first3=Marnin J.|date=September 2014|title=The Destructiveness of Perfectionism Revisited: Implications for the Assessment of Suicide Risk and the Prevention of Suicide|journal=Review of General Psychology|volume=18|issue=3|pages=156–172|doi=10.1037/gpr0000011|s2cid=144608904|issn=1089-2680}}</ref><ref name=":1" /><ref name="Smith 103954">{{Cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=Martin M.|last2=Sherry|first2=Simon B.|last3=Vidovic|first3=Vanja|last4=Hewitt|first4=Paul L.|last5=Flett|first5=Gordon L.|date=June 2020|title=Why does perfectionism confer risk for depressive symptoms? A meta-analytic test of the mediating role of stress and social disconnection|journal=Journal of Research in Personality|volume=86|article-number=103954|doi=10.1016/j.jrp.2020.103954|s2cid=216204822 |issn=0092-6566|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/4546/1/Smith.Sherry.Vidovic.Hewitt.Flett.2020.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Citation|last1=Hewitt|first1=Paul L.|chapter=Trait Perfectionism Dimensions and Suicidal Behavior.|date=2006|chapter-url=http://content.apa.org/books/11377-010|title=Cognition and suicide: Theory, research, and therapy.|pages=215–235|editor-last=Ellis|editor-first=Thomas E.|place=Washington|publisher=American Psychological Association|language=en|doi=10.1037/11377-010|isbn=978-1-59147-357-2|access-date=18 August 2020|last2=Flett|first2=Gordon L.|last3=Sherry|first3=Simon B.|last4=Caelian|first4=Carmen|archive-date=10 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201010052034/https://content.apa.org/record/2006-01745-010|url-status=live|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Measurement==

===Multidimensional perfectionism scale (MPS)===
Randy O. Frost et al. (1990) developed a multidimensional perfectionism scale (now known as the "Frost Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale", FMPS) with six dimensions:<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Frost | first1 = Randy O. | last2 = Marten | first2 = Patricia | last3 = Lahart | first3 = Cathleen | last4 = Rosenblate | first4 = Robin | year = 1990 | title = The dimensions of perfectionism | journal = Cognitive Therapy and Research | volume = 14 | issue = 5| pages = 449–468 | doi = 10.1007/BF01172967 | s2cid = 11748385 }}</ref>
#Concern over making mistakes
#High personal standards (striving for excellence)
#The perception of high parental expectations
#The perception of high parental criticism
#The doubting of the quality of one's actions, and
#A preference for order and organization.

Hewitt & Flett (1991) devised another "multidimensional perfectionism scale", a 45-item measure that rates three aspects of perfectionist self-presentation:<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal
 | last1 = Hewitt
 | first1 = P.
 | last2 = Flett
 | first2 = G.
 | title = Dimensions of Perfectionism in Unipolar Depression
 | journal = Journal of Abnormal Psychology
 | volume = 100
 | issue = 1
 | pages = 98–101
 | year = 1991
 | url = http://hewittlab.psych.ubc.ca/pdfs/1991hf1.pdf
 | doi = 10.1037/0021-843X.100.1.98
 | pmid = 2005279
 | access-date = 18 April 2008
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20140327054913/http://hewittlab.psych.ubc.ca/pdfs/1991hf1.pdf
 | archive-date = 27 March 2014
| url-status = dead
 }}</ref>
# Self-oriented perfectionism
# Other-oriented perfectionism, and
# Socially prescribed perfectionism.

Self-oriented perfectionism refers to having unrealistic expectations and standards for oneself that lead to perfectionist motivation.<ref name="autogenerated2">{{cite web|title=The Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale: Reliability, validity, and psychometric properties in psychiatric samples |url=http://www.mendeley.com/research/multidimensional-perfectionism-scale-reliability-validity-psychometric-properties-psychiatric-samples-1 |access-date=3 March 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121212005244/http://www.mendeley.com/research/multidimensional-perfectionism-scale-reliability-validity-psychometric-properties-psychiatric-samples-1 |archive-date=12 December 2012 }}</ref> Other-oriented perfectionism is having unrealistic expectations and standards for others that in turn pressure them to have perfectionist motivations of their own. Socially prescribed perfectionism is characterized by developing perfectionist motivations due actual or perceived high expectations of significant others. Parents who push their children to be successful in certain endeavors (such as athletics or academics) provide an example of what often causes this type of perfectionism, as the children feel that they must meet their parents' lofty expectations.

A similarity has been pointed out among Frost's distinction between ''setting high standards for oneself'' and the level of ''concern over making mistakes in performance'' (the two most important dimensions of the FMPS) and Hewitt & Flett's distinction between ''self-oriented'' versus ''socially prescribed perfectionism''.<ref>Toon W. Taris, Ilona van Beek, Wilmar B. Schaufeli: "Why do perfectionists have a higher burnout risk than others? The mediational effect of workaholism". ''Romanian Journal of Applied Psychology'', 2010, Vol.12, No.1, pp. 1–7.</ref>

===Perfectionist Self-Presentation Scale (PSPS)===
Hewitt et al. (2003) developed the perfectionist Self-Presentation Scale (PSPS), a 27-item self-report measure assessing the three interpersonal, expressive components of the Comprehensive Model of Perfectionism.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal|last1=Hewitt|first1=Paul L.|last2=Flett|first2=Gordon L.|last3=Sherry|first3=Simon B.|last4=Habke|first4=Marie|last5=Parkin|first5=Melanie|last6=Lam|first6=Raymond W.|last7=McMurtry|first7=Bruce|last8=Ediger|first8=Evelyn|last9=Fairlie|first9=Paul|last10=Stein|first10=Murray B.|date=June 2003|title=The interpersonal expression of perfection: Perfectionistic self-presentation and psychological distress.|journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology|language=en|volume=84|issue=6|pages=1303–1325|doi=10.1037/0022-3514.84.6.1303|pmid=12793591|issn=1939-1315}}</ref> It includes three subscales pertaining to perfectionist self-presentation, i.e., to the need to appear flawless:

#Perfectionist self-promotion
#Non-display of imperfection
#Nondisclosure of imperfection

The PSPS measures the expression (the process) of the trait of perfectionism and is directly linked to the perfectionism traits, particularly self-oriented and socially prescribed perfectionism. Additionally, the dimensions of the PSPS correlate with measures of [[Mental distress|psychological distress]], such as anxiety symptoms, indicating that perfectionist self-presentation is a maladaptive, defensive tendency.<ref name=":14" />

===Perfectionism Cognitions Inventory (PCI)===
The Perfectionism Cognitions Inventory (PCI) developed by Flett, Hewitt, Blankstein, and Gray (1998) is a 25-item inventory measuring the self-relational, cognitive component of perfectionism in the form of automatic thoughts about attaining perfection.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last1=Flett|first1=Gordon L.|last2=Hewitt|first2=Paul L.|last3=Demerjian|first3=Aline|last4=Sturman|first4=Edward D.|last5=Sherry|first5=Simon B.|last6=Cheng|first6=Winnie|date=June 2012|title=Perfectionistic Automatic Thoughts and Psychological Distress in Adolescents: An Analysis of the Perfectionism Cognitions Inventory|journal=Journal of Rational-Emotive & Cognitive-Behavior Therapy|language=en|volume=30|issue=2|pages=91–104|doi=10.1007/s10942-011-0131-7|s2cid=143619593|issn=0894-9085}}</ref> It includes statements about perfectionism-themed cognitions, such as references to social comparison and awareness of being imperfect and failing to attain high expectations.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Flett|first1=Gordon L.|last2=Hewitt|first2=Paul L.|last3=Blankstein|first3=Kirk R.|last4=Gray|first4=Lisa|date=1998|title=Psychological distress and the frequency of perfectionistic thinking.|journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology|language=en|volume=75|issue=5|pages=1363–1381|doi=10.1037/0022-3514.75.5.1363|pmid=9866193|issn=1939-1315}}</ref> Rather than emphasizing trait-like statements, the PCI is characterized by state-like statements, focusing on the varying situational and temporal contexts that can lead to different perfectionist thoughts.<ref name=":2" />

The PCI is associated with the presence of negative automatic thoughts and scoring high on this measure has been linked to a high degree of self-criticism, self-blame and failure perseveration.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Flett|first1=Gordon L.|last2=Hewitt|first2=Paul L.|last3=Whelan|first3=Teresa|last4=Martin|first4=Thomas R.|date=2 November 2007|title=The Perfectionism Cognitions Inventory: Psychometric Properties and Associations with Distress and Deficits in Cognitive Self-management|journal=Journal of Rational-Emotive & Cognitive-Behavior Therapy|language=en|volume=25|issue=4|pages=255–277|doi=10.1007/s10942-007-0055-4|s2cid=52268846|issn=0894-9085}}</ref>

=== Almost perfect scale-revised (APS-R) ===
Slaney and his colleagues (1996) developed the ''Almost Perfect Scale-Revised (APS-R)''.<ref name="Slaney-2001">{{Cite journal
 | last1 = Slaney | first1 = R.B.
 | last2 = Rice | first2 = K.G.
 | last3 = Mobley | first3 = M.
 | last4 = Trippi | first4 = J.
 | last5 = Ashby | first5 = J.S.
 | title = The Revised Almost Perfect Scale
 | journal = Measurement and Evaluation in Counseling and Development
 | volume = 34 | issue = 3 | pages = 130–145
 | year = 2001
 | doi = 10.1080/07481756.2002.12069030
 | s2cid = 148704959
 }}</ref> People are classified based on their scores for three measures:
#High Standards
#Order, and
#Discrepancy

Discrepancy refers to the belief that personal high standards are not being met, which is the defining negative aspect of perfectionism.<ref name="Slaney-2001" /> Those with high scores in what the APS-R considers maladaptive perfectionism typically yield the highest [[social stress]] and anxiety scores, reflecting their feelings of inadequacy and low self-esteem.<ref name="Rice, Ashby, & Gilman" /> However, whether high standards as measured by APS-R actually assess perfectionism is debatable.<ref name=":3"/><ref name=":7">{{Cite journal|last=Gaudreau|first=Patrick|date=21 November 2018|title=On the Distinction Between Personal Standards Perfectionism and Excellencism: A Theory Elaboration and Research Agenda|journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science|volume=14|issue=2|pages=197–215|doi=10.1177/1745691618797940|pmid=30462927|s2cid=53722672|issn=1745-6916}}</ref>

In general, the APS-R is a relatively easy instrument to administer, and can be used to identify perfectionist adolescents as well as adults, though it has yet to be proven useful for children.<ref name="Rice, Ashby, & Gilman">{{cite journal|last=Rice|first=Kenneth G.|author2=Ashby, Jeffrey S. |author3=Gilman, Rich |title=Classifying adolescent perfectionists|journal=Psychological Assessment|year=2011|volume=23|issue=3|pages=563–577|doi=10.1037/a0022482|pmid=21319903}}</ref> Two other forms of the APS-R measure perfectionism directed towards intimate partners (Dyadic Almost Perfect Scale) and perceived perfectionism from one's family (Family Almost Perfect Scale).

The validity of the APS-R has been challenged. Namely, some researchers maintain that high standards are not necessarily perfectionist standards.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":7"/> For instance, it has been shown that when the APS-R is re-worded to reflect more perfectionist terms, outcomes differ in comparison to the original wording of this scale.<ref name=":3" /> Specifically, only the reworded, more perfectionist scale is associated with maladjustment, such as depression and anxiety, while only the original scale is related to adaptive outcomes.<ref name=":3" /> This suggests that what is labelled as "adaptive perfectionism" in the original APS-R may simply reflect high standards. Moreover, a number of researchers view the relevance of discrepancy to the perfectionism literature as suspect given the number of negative mood terms included. Including negative mood terms in items, such as the discrepancy subscale, greatly increases the likelihood for discovering a relation between perfectionism and neuroticism which may be simply due to wording rather than a perfectionism-neuroticism link.<ref name="Smith 367–390">{{Cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=Martin M.|last2=Sherry|first2=Simon B.|last3=Vidovic|first3=Vanja|last4=Saklofske|first4=Donald H.|last5=Stoeber|first5=Joachim|last6=Benoit|first6=Aryn|date=6 January 2019|title=Perfectionism and the Five-Factor Model of Personality: A Meta-Analytic Review|journal=Personality and Social Psychology Review|volume=23|issue=4|pages=367–390|doi=10.1177/1088868318814973|pmid=30612510|s2cid=58632915|issn=1088-8683|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/3563/1/Smith.Sherry.Vidovic.Saklofske.Stoeber.Benoit.in%20press.pdf|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=2 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190502012148/https://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/3563/1/Smith.Sherry.Vidovic.Saklofske.Stoeber.Benoit.in%20press.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Physical appearance perfectionism scale (PAPS)===
The ''Physical Appearance Perfectionism Scale (PAPS)'' explains a particular type of perfectionism: the desire for a perfect physical appearance.<ref name="Yang & Stoeber">{{cite journal|last=Yang|first=Hongfei|author2=Stoeber, Joachim|title=The Physical Appearance Perfectionism Scale: Development and Preliminary Validation|journal=Journal of Psychopathology and Behavioral Assessment|year=2012|volume=34|issue=1|pages=69–83|doi=10.1007/s10862-011-9260-7|s2cid=53542541|url=http://kar.kent.ac.uk/28120/1/Yang%20Stoeber%20%282012%29%20JPBA.pdf|access-date=5 February 2019|archive-date=19 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180719035130/https://kar.kent.ac.uk/28120/1/Yang%20Stoeber%20(2012)%20JPBA.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> The PAPS is a multidimensional assessment of physical appearance perfectionism that provides the most insight when the sub-scales are evaluated separately.<ref name="Yang & Stoeber" />

In general, the PAPS allows researchers to determine participants' [[body image]] and self-conceptions of their looks, which is critical in present times when so much attention is paid to attractiveness and obtaining the ideal appearance.<ref name="Yang & Stoeber" /> The two sub-scales it uses to assess appearance concerns are:
# Worry About Imperfection, and
# Hope For Perfection.

Those that obtain high "Worry About Imperfection" scores are usually greatly concerned with attaining perfection, physical appearance, and body control behavior.<ref name="Yang & Stoeber" /> They also demonstrate low positive self-perceptions of their appearance, whereas those scoring highly on "Hope for Perfection" yielded high positive self-perceptions.<ref name="Yang & Stoeber" /> Hope For Perfection also corresponded with impression management behaviors and striving for ambitious goals.

In summary, Worry About Imperfection relates to negative aspects of appearance perfectionism, while Hope For Perfection relates to positive aspects. One limitation of using the PAPS is the lack of psychological literature evaluating its validity.<ref name="Yang & Stoeber" />

==Psychological implications==
Perfectionists tend to dissociate themselves from their flaws or what they believe are flaws (such as negative emotions) and can become hypocritical and hypercritical of others, seeking the illusion of virtue to hide their own vices.<ref>{{Cite book
 | last1= Daniels, M.D. |first1= D.
 | last2= Price, PhD |first2= V.
 | title= The Essential Enneagram
 | place = New York
 | publisher = HarperCollins
 | year = 2000
 | isbn = 978-0062516763
 }}</ref>

Researchers have begun to investigate the role of perfectionism in various mental disorders such as [[Depression (mood)|depression]],<ref name="Smith 103954"/> [[anxiety]], [[eating disorders]],<ref name=":9" /> [[autism]]<ref>{{cite journal|title=Dysfunctional attitudes and perfectionism and their relationship to anxious and depressive symptoms in boys with autism spectrum disorders|last1=Greenaway |first1=R |last2=Howlin |first2=P |journal=[[Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders]]|date=25 February 2010 |volume=40 |issue=10 |pages=1179–1187|doi=10.1007/s10803-010-0977-z|pmid=20182783 }}
</ref> and [[personality disorders]], as well as suicide.<ref name=":6" /><ref name="Smith 522–542"/><ref name=":10" /> Each disorder is associated with varying levels of the three subscales on the Multidimensional Perfectionism Scale.<ref name="autogenerated2" /> For instance, socially prescribed perfectionism in young women has been associated with greater body-image dissatisfaction and avoidance of social situations that focus on weight and physical appearance.<ref name="Hewitt">{{cite journal|last=Hewitt|first=P. L.|author2=Flett, G. |author3=Ediger, E. |title=Perfectionism traits and perfectionistic self-presentation in eating disorder attitudes, characteristics, and symptoms|journal=International Journal of Eating Disorders|year=1995|volume=18|pages=317–326|doi=10.1002/1098-108X(199512)18:4<317::AID-EAT2260180404>3.0.CO;2-2|pmid=8580917|issue=4}}</ref>

The relationship that exists between perfectionist tendencies and methods of coping with stress has also been examined in some detail. Those who displayed tendencies associated with perfectionism, such as rumination over past events or fixation on mistakes, tended to utilize more passive or [[avoidance coping]].<ref name=":0">{{cite journal|last1=Wielkiewicz|first1=R. M.|last2=Wonderlich|first2=S. J.|year=2006|title=Correlations between perfectionism and coping strategies in response to researcher-selected vignettes or participant-selected events|journal=Psychological Reports|volume=98|issue=3|pages=745–755|doi=10.2466/pr0.98.3.745-755|pmid=16933672|s2cid=26569485}}</ref> They also tended to utilize [[Self-criticism#Neuroscience|self-criticism]] as a coping method.<ref name=":0" /> This is consistent with theories that conceptualize self-criticism as a central element of perfectionism.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Dunkley |first1=David M. |last2=Zuroff |first2=David C. |last3=Blankstein |first3=Kirk R. |year=2003 |title=Self-critical perfectionism and daily affect: dispositional and situational influences on stress and coping |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |volume=84 |number=1 |pages=234–252 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.84.1.234 |pmid=12518982 |s2cid=88727 }}</ref>

== Consequences ==
Perfectionism can be damaging. It can take the form of [[procrastination]] when used to postpone tasks and [[self-deprecation]] when used to excuse poor performance or to seek sympathy and affirmation from other people. These, together or separate, are [[self-handicapping]] strategies perfectionists may use to protect their sense of self-competence.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Jones|first1=E.E.|last2=Berglas|first2=S.|date=1978|title=Control of attributions about the self through selfhandicapping strategies: The appeal of alcohol and the role of underachievement|url=http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ837977|journal=Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin|volume=35|issue=3|pages=200–206|doi=10.1177/014616727800400205|s2cid=146420423|access-date=15 June 2016|archive-date=8 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160808170318/http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ837977|url-status=live|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kearns|first1=Hugh|last2=Forbes|first2=Angus|last3=Gardiner|first3=Maria|last4=Marshall|first4=Kelly|date=December 2008|title=When a High Distinction Isn't Good Enough: A Review of Perfectionism and Self-Handicapping|url=http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ837977|journal=Australian Educational Researcher|volume=35|issue=3|pages=21–36|access-date=15 June 2016|archive-date=8 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160808170318/http://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ837977|url-status=live}}</ref> In general, perfectionists feel constant pressure to meet their high expectations, which creates [[cognitive dissonance]] when expectations cannot be met. Perfectionism has been associated with numerous other psychological and physiological complications. Moreover, perfectionism may result in alienation and social disconnection via certain rigid interpersonal patterns common to perfectionist individuals.<ref name=":1" />

===Suicide===
Perfectionism is increasingly considered to be a [[risk factor]] for [[suicide]].<ref name="Smith 522–542" /> The tendency of perfectionists to have excessively high expectations of self and to be self-critical when their efforts do not meet the expectations they have established, combined with their tendency to present a public image of flawlessness increases their risk of [[suicidal ideation]] while decreasing the likelihood of seeking help when it is needed.<ref>Greenspon, Thomas S. "Is There an Antidote to Perfectionism?" ''Psychology in the Schools'', November 2014: 986–998.</ref> Perfectionism is one of many suicide predictors that affect individuals negatively via pressure to fulfill other- or self-generated high expectations, feeling incapable of living up to them, and social disconnection.<ref name="Smith 522–542" />

Importantly, the relation between suicidality and perfectionism depends on the particular perfectionism dimensions. Perfectionist strivings are associated with suicidal ideation while perfectionist concerns are predictive of both suicidal ideation and attempting suicide.<ref name="Smith 522–542" /> Additionally, socially prescribed perfectionism, a type of perfectionist concern, was found to be associated with both baseline and long-term suicidal ideation.<ref name="Smith 522–542" /> This implies that perfectionist concerns, such as socially prescribed perfectionism, are related to more pernicious outcomes in the context of suicide.<ref name="Smith 522–542" />

=== Anorexia nervosa ===
Perfectionism has been linked with [[anorexia nervosa]] in research for decades. Researchers in 1949 described the behavior of the average anorexic person as being "rigid" and "hyperconscious", observing also a tendency to "neatness, meticulosity, and a mulish stubbornness not amenable to reason [which] make her a rank perfectionist".<ref name=cachexia>{{cite journal|journal=American Journal of Psychiatry|last=DuBois|first=F.S.|year=1949|title=Compulsion neurosis with cachexia (Anorexia Nervosa)|volume=106|issue = 2|pages=107–115|doi=10.1176/ajp.106.2.107|pmid=18135398}}</ref> Perfectionism is an enduring characteristic in the biographies of anorexics. It is present before the onset of the eating disorder, generally in childhood,<ref name=Anderluh>{{cite journal|last=Anderluh|first=Marija Brecelj|title=Lifetime course of eating disorders: design and validity testing of a new strategy to define the eating disorders phenotype|year=2009|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/43245194|journal=Psychological Medicine|volume=39|issue=1|pages=105–114|doi=10.1017/S0033291708003292|pmid=18377676|s2cid=12871351|access-date=4 December 2017|archive-date=10 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201010052033/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/43245194_Lifetime_course_of_eating_disorders_Design_and_validity_testing_of_a_new_strategy_to_define_the_eating_disorders_phenotype|url-status=live}}</ref> during the illness,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Perfectionism in Anorexia Nervosa:Variation by Clinical Subtype, Obsessionality, and Pathological Eating Behavior|first1=Katherine A.|last1=Halmi|display-authors=etal|year=2000|journal=Am J Psychiatry|pages=1799–1805|volume=157|issue=11|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12269220|doi=10.1176/appi.ajp.157.11.1799|pmid=11058477|access-date=5 February 2019|archive-date=10 October 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201010052034/https://www.researchgate.net/publication/12269220_Perfectionism_in_Anorexia_Nervosa_Variation_by_Clinical_Subtype_Obsessionality_and_Pathological_Eating_Behavior|url-status=live}}</ref> and also, after remission.<ref name=persistent>{{cite journal|last=Srinivasagam|title=Persistent perfectionism, symmetry, and exactness after long-term recovery from anorexia nervosa|journal=American Journal of Psychiatry|year=1995|pmid=7485626|volume=152|issue=11|pages=1630–4|doi=10.1176/ajp.152.11.1630|citeseerx=10.1.1.457.3479|s2cid=10233035 }}</ref> The incessant striving for thinness among anorexics is itself a manifestation of this personality style, of an insistence upon meeting unattainably high standards of performance.<ref name=school />

Because of its chronicity, those with eating disorders also display perfectionist tendencies in other domains of life than [[dieting]] and weight control. Over-achievement at school, for example, has been observed among anorexics,<ref name=school /><ref>{{cite journal|title=The Significance of Bulimia in Juvenile Anorexia Nervosa: An Exploration of Possible Etiologic Factors|year=1981|journal=International Journal of Eating Disorders|author=Michael Strober|volume=1|issue=1|pages=28–43|doi=10.1002/1098-108x(198123)1:1<28::aid-eat2260010104>3.0.co;2-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Primary Anorexia Nervosa|year=1979|author=D. L. Norris |journal=South African Medical Journal|pages=987–93}}</ref> as a result of their overly industrious behavior.<ref name=school>{{cite journal|title=Differences between IQ and school achievement in anorexia nervosa|year=1989|journal=Journal of Clinical Psychology|author=JR Dura|volume=45|pages=433–5|pmid=2745732|issue=3|doi=10.1002/1097-4679(198905)45:3<433::aid-jclp2270450313>3.0.co;2-x|display-authors=etal}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=The Golden Cage: The Enigma of Anorexia Nervosa|url=https://archive.org/details/goldencageenigma00bruc_0|url-access=registration|author=Hilde Bruch|year=2001|publisher=First Harvard University Press|page=[https://archive.org/details/goldencageenigma00bruc_0/page/46 46]|isbn=9780674005846 |author-link=Hilde Bruch}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=L'anorexie mentale, une déraison philosophique|author=Bernard Viallettes|year=2001|isbn=978-2-7475-0876-6|publisher=L'Harmattan|quote=...even in the category of young women with low IQs, some had brilliant school records. This probably is the result of the persistence in work that characterizes anorexic patients.|page=89}}</ref>

The level of perfectionism was found to have an influence on individual's long-term recovery of anorexia. Those who scored a lower range of perfectionism were able to have a faster recovery rate than patients who scored high in perfectionism.<ref>Sutandar-Pinnock, K., Woodside, D.B., Carter, J.C., Olmsted, M.P., and Kaplan, A.S. (2003). Perfectionism in Anorexia Nervosa: A 6-24-month follow-up study. International Journal of Eating Disorders, 33(2). 1. {{doi|10.1002/eat.10127}}.</ref>

===General applications===
Perfectionism often shows up in performance at work or school, neatness and aesthetics, organization, writing, speaking, physical appearance, and health and personal cleanliness.<ref name="Antony">{{cite book|last=Antony, PhD|first=Martin|title=When Perfect Isn't Good Enough: Strategies for Coping with Perfectionism|year=2009|publisher=New Harbinger Publications|location=Oakland, CA|isbn=978-1572245594|pages=312}}</ref> In the workplace, perfectionism is often marked by low [[productivity]] and missed deadlines as people lose time and energy by paying attention to irrelevant details of their tasks, ranging from major projects to mundane daily activities. This can lead to [[Clinical depression|depression]], [[social alienation]], and a greater risk of workplace "accidents".<ref>{{Cite news
 | last = Psychology Today
 | title = Perfectionism: Impossible Dream
 | newspaper = Psychology Today
 | date = May 1995
 | url = http://www.psychologytoday.com/articles/199505/perfectionism-impossible-dream
 | access-date = 15 May 2012
| archive-date = 10 October 2020
| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20201010052035/https://www.psychologytoday.com/intl/articles/199505/perfectionism-impossible-dream
 | url-status = live
 }}</ref> Adderholdt-Elliot (1989) describes five characteristics of perfectionist students and teachers which contribute to underachievement: procrastination, fear of failure, an [[Splitting (psychology)|"all-or-nothing" mindset]], paralyzed perfectionism, and [[workaholism]].<ref>{{Cite journal
 | last = Adderholdt-Elliot | first = M.
 | title = Perfectionism and underachievement
 | journal = Gifted Child Today
 | volume = 12 | issue = 1 | pages = 19–21
 | year = 1989
 | doi = 10.1177/107621758901200108
 | s2cid = 220183463
 }}</ref>

According to C. Allen, in intimate relationships, unrealistic expectations can cause significant dissatisfaction for both partners.<ref>{{Cite news
 | last = Allen | first = C.
 | title = The Perfectionist's Flawed Marriage
 | newspaper = Psychology Today
 | date = May 2003
 | url = http://www.psychologytoday.com/articles/200002/the-perfectionists-flawed-marriage
 }}</ref> Greenspon lists behaviors, thoughts, and feelings that typically characterize perfectionism.<ref name="Greenspon, T. S. 2002">{{self-published inline|date=November 2017}}Greenspon, T. S. (2002) ''Freeing Our Families From Perfectionism''. Minneapolis: Free Spirit Publishing.</ref> Perfectionists will not be content with their work until it meets their standards, which can make perfectionists less efficient in finishing projects, and they therefore will struggle to meet deadlines.

In a different occupational context, athletes may develop perfectionist tendencies. Optimal physical and mental performance is critical for professional athletes, which are aspects that closely relate to perfectionism. Although perfectionist athletes strive to succeed, they can be limited by their intense fear of failure and therefore not exert themselves fully or feel overly personally responsible for a loss.<ref name="Perfectionism Sports">{{cite web|title=The Downside of Perfectionism in Sports|date=23 March 2011 |url=http://www.sportpsychologytoday.com/youth-sports-psychology/the-downside-of-perfectionism-in-sports/|publisher=Sports Psychology Today|access-date=12 May 2012|archive-date=2 May 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120502162325/http://www.sportpsychologytoday.com/youth-sports-psychology/the-downside-of-perfectionism-in-sports/|url-status=live}}</ref> Because their success is frequently measured by a score or statistics, perfectionist athletes may feel excessive pressure to succeed.

===Medical complications===
Perfectionism is a risk factor for [[obsessive–compulsive disorder]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Wu|first1=Kevin D.|last2=Cortesi|first2=Gina T.|date=April 2009|title=Relations between perfectionism and obsessive–compulsive symptoms: Examination of specificity among the dimensions|journal=Journal of Anxiety Disorders|volume=23|issue=3|pages=393–400|doi=10.1016/j.janxdis.2008.11.006|pmid=19110399|issn=0887-6185}}</ref> [[obsessive–compulsive personality disorder]], [[eating disorders]],<ref name=":9" /> [[social anxiety]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jain|first1=Mansi|last2=Sudhir|first2=Paulomi M.|date=December 2010|title=Dimensions of perfectionism and perfectionistic self-presentation in social phobia|journal=Asian Journal of Psychiatry|volume=3|issue=4|pages=216–221|doi=10.1016/j.ajp.2010.08.006|pmid=23050891|issn=1876-2018}}</ref> [[body dysmorphic disorder]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Buhlmann|first1=Ulrike|last2=Etcoff|first2=Nancy L.|last3=Wilhelm|first3=Sabine|date=April 2008|title=Facial attractiveness ratings and perfectionism in body dysmorphic disorder and obsessive-compulsive disorder|journal=Journal of Anxiety Disorders|volume=22|issue=3|pages=540–547|doi=10.1016/j.janxdis.2007.05.004|pmid=17624717|issn=0887-6185}}</ref> [[workaholism]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Stoeber|first1=Joachim|last2=Davis|first2=Charlotte R.|last3=Townley|first3=Jessica|date=October 2013|title=Perfectionism and workaholism in employees: The role of work motivation|journal=Personality and Individual Differences|volume=55|issue=7|pages=733–738|doi=10.1016/j.paid.2013.06.001|issn=0191-8869|url=https://kar.kent.ac.uk/34044/1/Stoeber%20Davis%20Townley%20%282013%29%20PAID.pdf|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=2 November 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181102110008/https://kar.kent.ac.uk/34044/1/Stoeber%20Davis%20Townley%20(2013)%20PAID.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> [[self harm]] and suicide,<ref name="Smith 522–542" /> [[substance abuse]], and [[clinical depression]]<ref name=":12" /> as well as physical problems like [[heart disease]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Corson|first1=Ansley T.|last2=Loveless|first2=James P.|last3=Mochrie|first3=Kirk D.|last4=Whited|first4=Matthew C.|date=2 January 2018|title=Perfectionism in Relation to Stress and Cardiovascular Disease Among Gifted Individuals and the Need for Affective Interventions|journal=Roeper Review|volume=40|issue=1|pages=46–55|doi=10.1080/02783193.2017.1393711|s2cid=149326967|issn=0278-3193}}</ref> In addition, studies have found that people with perfectionism have a higher [[mortality rate]] than those without perfectionism.<ref name=":13" /> A possible reason for this is the additional stress and worry that accompanies the irrational belief that everything should be perfect.<ref name=":13" />

Therapists who attempt to tackle the negative thinking that surrounds perfectionism, in particular the [[Splitting (psychology)|"all-or-nothing" thinking]] in which the client believes that an achievement is either perfect or useless. They encourage clients to set realistic goals and to face their fear of failure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kelly |first=John D. |date=October 2015 |title=Your Best Life: Perfectionism—The Bane of Happiness |journal=Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research |volume=473 |issue=10 |pages=3108–3111 |doi=10.1007/s11999-015-4279-9 |issn=0009-921X |pmc=4562912 |pmid=25836762}}</ref>

Since perfectionism is a self-esteem issue based on emotional convictions about what one must do to be acceptable as a person, negative thinking is most successfully addressed in the context of a recovery process which directly addresses these convictions.<ref name="Greenspon-2008">{{cite journal|last1=Greenspon|first1=T. S.|year=2008|title=Making sense of error: A view of the origins and treatment of perfectionism|journal=American Journal of Psychotherapy|volume=62|issue=3|pages=263–282|doi=10.1176/appi.psychotherapy.2008.62.3.263|pmid=18846972|doi-access=free}}</ref>

=== Impact on psychological treatment ===
A number of studies suggest that perfectionism can limit the effectiveness of psychotherapy. Namely, perfectionism impedes treatment success across [[Help-seeking|seeking]], maintaining, and ultimately benefiting from help.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Hewitt|first1=Paul L.|last2=Habke|first2=A. Marie|last3=Lee-Baggley|first3=Dayna L.|last4=Sherry|first4=Simon B.|last5=Flett|first5=Gordon L.|date=June 2008|title=The Impact of Perfectionistic Self-Presentation on the Cognitive, Affective, and Physiological Experience of a Clinical Interview|journal=Psychiatry: Interpersonal and Biological Processes|volume=71|issue=2|pages=93–122|doi=10.1521/psyc.2008.71.2.93|pmid=18573033|s2cid=1364808|issn=0033-2747}}</ref>                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                Unfavourable attitudes and negative beliefs towards seeking help present a barrier to treatment among perfectionists.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Dang|first1=Silvain S.|last2=Quesnel|first2=Danika A.|last3=Hewitt|first3=Paul L.|last4=Flett|first4=Gordon L.|last5=Deng|first5=Xiaolei|date=8 April 2020|title=Perfectionistic traits and self-presentation are associated with negative attitudes and concerns about seeking professional psychological help|journal=Clinical Psychology & Psychotherapy|volume=27|issue=5|pages=621–629|language=en|doi=10.1002/cpp.2450|pmid=32222088|s2cid=214695286 }}</ref> When they do attend treatment, perfectionists, especially those high in perfectionist self-presentation, are more likely to experience initial clinical interviews as anxiety-provoking and appraise their performance as inadequate.<ref name=":4" /> Perfectionism can also affect treatment adherence. For example, a study demonstrated that other-oriented perfectionism is associated with treatment attrition.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=McCown|first1=William G.|last2=Carlson|first2=Glen|date=2004|title=Narcissism, Perfectionism, and Self-Termination from Treatment in Outpatient Cocaine Users|journal=Journal of Rational-Emotive & Cognitive-Behavior Therapy|volume=22|issue=4|pages=325–336|doi=10.1023/b:jore.0000047314.90953.c9|s2cid=143332969|issn=0894-9085}}</ref> Further, treatment effectiveness may be compromised by perfectionists' tendency to present an image of flawlessness and avoid self-disclosures because of an excessive sensitivity to judgment and rejection.<ref name=":11" /> Most importantly, treatment success may be negatively impacted due to the interpersonal disconnection prevalent among perfectionists which is associated with a failure to develop or strengthen a positive therapeutic alliance.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hewitt|first1=Paul L.|last2=Smith|first2=Martin M.|last3=Deng|first3=Xiaolei|last4=Chen|first4=Chang|last5=Ko|first5=Ariel|last6=Flett|first6=Gordon L.|last7=Paterson|first7=Randy J.|date=June 2020|title=The perniciousness of perfectionism in group therapy for depression: A test of the perfectionism social disconnection model.|journal=Psychotherapy|language=en|volume=57|issue=2|pages=206–218|doi=10.1037/pst0000281|pmid=31999191|s2cid=210947283 |issn=1939-1536|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/4187/1/Psychotherapy%20Paper%202019.pdf|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=8 May 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200508141003/https://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/4187/1/Psychotherapy%20Paper%202019.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":11"/>

== Narcissism ==
According to [[Arnold Cooper]], [[narcissism]] can be considered as a self-perceived form of perfectionism – "an insistence on perfection in the idealized self-object and the limitless power of the grandiose self. These are rooted in traumatic injuries to the grandiose self."<ref name="Arnold M. Cooper 2006">Arnold M. Cooper, "Introduction"  in Arnold M. Cooper ed., ''Contemporary Psychoanalysis in America'' (2006) p. xxxiv</ref> In support, research suggests some forms of perfectionism are associated with grandiose narcissism while others are associated with vulnerable narcissism.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Smith|first1=Martin M.|last2=Sherry|first2=Simon B.|last3=Chen|first3=Samantha|last4=Saklofske|first4=Donald H.|last5=Flett|first5=Gordon L.|last6=Hewitt|first6=Paul L.|date=October 2016|title=Perfectionism and narcissism: A meta-analytic review|journal=Journal of Research in Personality|volume=64|pages=90–101|doi=10.1016/j.jrp.2016.07.012|issn=0092-6566|url=http://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2907/1/Smith.Sherry.Chen.Saklofske.Flett.Hewitt.JRP.2016.pdf|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=1 May 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190501235541/https://ray.yorksj.ac.uk/id/eprint/2907/1/Smith.Sherry.Chen.Saklofske.Flett.Hewitt.JRP.2016.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> Similar to perfectionism, narcissism, particularly in its vulnerable form, is associated with a contingent self-worth and a need for validation.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Pincus|first1=A. L.|last2=Ansell|first2=E. B.|last3=Pimentel|first3=C. A.|last4=Cain|first4=N. M.|last5=Wright|first5=A. G. C.|last6=Levy|first6=K . N.|date=2009|title=Initial construction and validation of the Pathological Narcissism Inventory|journal=Psychological Assessment|volume=21|issue=3|pages=365–379|doi=10.1037/a0016530|pmid=19719348}}</ref> Narcissists often are pseudo-perfectionists and require being the center of attention and create situations where they will receive attention. This attempt at being perfect is cohesive with the narcissist's grandiose self-image.<ref name="Sorotzkin2005">{{cite web|last=Sorotzkin|first=Benzion|date=18 April 2006|title=The Quest for Perfection: Avoiding Guilt or avoiding shame?|url=http://www.drsorotzkin.com/quest_for_perfection.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080309214032/http://www.drsorotzkin.com/quest_for_perfection.html|archive-date=9 March 2008|work=[[Psychology Today]]|publisher=Sussex Publishers|location=New York City}}</ref> Behind such perfectionism, [[self psychology]] would see earlier traumatic injuries to the [[Grandiosity|grandiose]] self.<ref name="Arnold M. Cooper 2006"/>

Vulnerable narcissism is mostly covert and is characterized by a need for other people's recognition (e.g., validation or admiration) and a sense of self-worth that is contingent upon this recognition.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal|last1=Stoeber|first1=Joachim|last2=Sherry|first2=Simon B.|last3=Nealis|first3=Logan J.|date=July 2015|title=Multidimensional perfectionism and narcissism: Grandiose or vulnerable?|journal=Personality and Individual Differences|volume=80|pages=85–90|doi=10.1016/j.paid.2015.02.027|s2cid=16157388 |issn=0191-8869|url=https://kar.kent.ac.uk/47300/1/Stoeber%20Sherry%20Nealis%20%282015%29%20PAID.pdf|access-date=1 September 2020|archive-date=20 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180720175104/https://kar.kent.ac.uk/47300/1/Stoeber%20Sherry%20Nealis%20(2015)%20PAID.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> If a perceived state of perfection is not attained and recognition is not forthcoming or doubtful, this can result in a lowered self-worth, social withdrawal and avoidance behaviours as the individual fear that he or she will lose validation and [[Narcissistic supply|admiration]].<ref name=":8" />

==Personality traits==
Perfectionism is one of [[Raymond Cattell]]'s [[16 Personality Factors]].<ref name="Cattell-2008">{{Cite book
 | last1 = Cattell
 | first1 = H.
 | last2 = Mead
 | first2 = A.
 | chapter = The Sixteen Personality Factor Questionnaire (16PF)
 | title = The SAGE Handbook of Personality Theory and Assessment
 | editor = Gregory J. Boyle
 | editor2 = Gerald Matthews
 | editor3 = Donald H. Saklofske
 | volume = 2
 | pages = 135–159
 | year = 2008
 | doi = 10.4135/9781849200479.n7
 | isbn = 9781412946520
 | s2cid = 16809893
 }}</ref> According to this construct, people who are organized, compulsive, self-disciplined, socially precise, exacting will power, controlled, and self-sentimental are perfectionists. In the [[Big Five personality traits]], perfectionism is an extreme manifestation of [[conscientiousness]] and can provoke increasing [[neuroticism]] as the perfectionist's expectations are not met.<ref name="Cattell-2008" />

Perfectionist concerns are more similar to [[neuroticism]] while perfectionist strivings are more similar to [[conscientiousness]].<ref name="Smith 367–390"/>

==Children and adolescents==
The prevalence of perfectionism is high in children and adolescents, with estimates ranging from 25% to 30%.<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal|last1=Flett|first1=Gordon L.|last2=Hewitt|first2=Paul L.|last3=Besser|first3=Avi|last4=Su|first4=Chang|last5=Vaillancourt|first5=Tracy|last6=Boucher|first6=Daniel|last7=Munro|first7=Yvette|last8=Davidson|first8=Lisa A.|last9=Gale|first9=Olga|date=October 2016|title=The Child–Adolescent Perfectionism Scale: Development, Psychometric Properties, and Associations With Stress, Distress, and Psychiatric Symptoms|journal=Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment|language=en|volume=34|issue=7|pages=634–652|doi=10.1177/0734282916651381|s2cid=148186602|issn=0734-2829}}</ref> Similar to adults, perfectionism in young people is a core vulnerability factor for a variety of negative outcomes, such as depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.<ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ye |first1=Huan J. |last2=Rice |first2=Kenneth G. |last3=Storch |first3=Eric A. |date=2008 |title=Perfectionism and Peer Relations for Children With Obsessive--Compulsive Disorder |journal=Child Psychiatry and Human Development |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=415–426 |doi=10.1037/e528222007-001 |pmid=18338246 }}</ref> In order to measure the two trait components of self-oriented and socially prescribed perfectionism in this age group, the widely used Child-Adolescent Perfectionism Scale (CAPS) can be useful.<ref name=":5" />

==Treatments==

=== Cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) ===
[[Cognitive behavioral therapy|Cognitive-behavioral therapy]] (CBT) has been shown to successfully help perfectionists in reducing social anxiety, public self-consciousness, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) behaviors, and perfectionism.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Lundh|first1=Lars-Gunnar|last2=Ost|first2=Lars-Goran|date=5 November 2010|title=Attentional Bias, Self-consciousness and Perfectionism in Social Phobia Before and After Cognitive-Behaviour Therapy|journal=Scandinavian Journal of Behaviour Therapy | volume = 30| issue = 1|doi=10.1080/02845710117841|pages=4–16|s2cid=218574709}}</ref> By using this approach, a person can begin to recognize their irrational thinking and find an alternative way to approach situations.

=== Psychodynamic/interpersonal therapy (PI) ===
Consistent with the development and expression of perfectionism within an interpersonal context, this treatment focuses on the dynamic-relational basis of perfectionism. Rather than targeting perfectionist behaviour directly and aiming merely for symptom reduction, dynamic-relational therapy is characterized by a focus on the maladaptive relational patterns and interpersonal dynamics underlying and maintaining perfectionism.<ref name=":1" /> According to research by Hewitt et al. (2015), this form of treatment is associated with long-lasting reductions in both perfectionism and associated distress.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hewitt|first1=Paul L.|last2=Mikail|first2=Samuel F.|last3=Flett|first3=Gordon L.|last4=Tasca|first4=Giorgio A.|last5=Flynn|first5=Carol A.|last6=Deng|first6=Xiaolei|last7=Kaldas|first7=Janet|last8=Chen|first8=Chang|date=2015|title=Psychodynamic/interpersonal group psychotherapy for perfectionism: Evaluating the effectiveness of a short-term treatment.|journal=Psychotherapy|volume=52|issue=2|pages=205–217|doi=10.1037/pst0000016|pmid=25985044|issn=1939-1536}}</ref>

=== Exposure and response prevention (ERP) ===
[[Exposure therapy|Exposure and response prevention]] (ERP) is also employed by psychologists in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive symptoms, including perfectionism. This form of therapy is premised on encouraging individuals to stop their perfectionist behavior in tasks that they would normally pursue toward perfection. Over time, anxiety may decrease as the person finds that there are no major consequences of completing particular tasks imperfectly.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Strategies for Coping with the Need to be Perfect|url=https://beyondocd.org/expert-perspectives/articles/the-search-for-imperfection-strategies-for-coping-with-the-need-to-be-perfe|access-date=4 July 2020|website=Beyond OCD|language=en-US|archive-date=4 July 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200704103215/https://beyondocd.org/expert-perspectives/articles/the-search-for-imperfection-strategies-for-coping-with-the-need-to-be-perfe|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Acceptance-based behavior therapy (ABBT) ===
Acceptance-based behavior therapy (ABBT) was demonstrated to have a major contribution to treat perfectionism from increasing awareness, increasing acceptance, and living a meaningful life.<ref name="Ashbaugh, A. 2007">Ashbaugh, A., Antony, M.M., Liss, A., Summerfeldt, L.J., McCabe, R.E., & Swinson, R.P. (2007). Changes in perfectionism following cognitive-behavioral therapy of social phobia. Depression and Anxiety, 24, 169-177.</ref> These practices were shown to help reduce anxiety, depression, and social phobia. This approach has been shown to be effective six months post to the therapy.<ref name="Ashbaugh, A. 2007" /><ref>Pleva, J., & Wade, T.D. (2006). Guided self-help versus pure self-help for perfectionism: A randomised controlled trial. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 45, 849-861.</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Personality
