======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Personality neuroscience
======================================================================

'''Personality neuroscience''' uses neuroscientific methods to study the neurobiological mechanisms underlying individual differences in stable psychological attributes. Specifically, personality neuroscience aims to investigate the relationships between inter-individual variation in brain structures as well as functions and behavioral measures of persistent psychological traits, broadly defined as "predispositions and average tendencies to be in particular states", including but are not limited to personality traits, sociobehavioral tendencies, and psychopathological risk factors.<ref name="DeYoung-2022">{{Cite journal |last1=DeYoung |first1=Colin G. |last2=Beaty |first2=Roger E. |last3=Genç |first3=Erhan |last4=Latzman |first4=Robert D. |last5=Passamonti |first5=Luca |last6=Servaas |first6=Michelle N. |last7=Shackman |first7=Alexander J. |last8=Smillie |first8=Luke D. |last9=Spreng |first9=R. Nathan |last10=Viding |first10=Essi |last11=Wacker |first11=Jan |date=2022-10-12 |title=Personality neuroscience: An emerging field with bright prospects |url=https://ps.psychopen.eu/index.php/ps/article/view/7269 |journal=[[Personality Science]] |volume=3 |article-number=e7269 |doi=10.5964/ps.7269 |issn=2700-0710 |pmc=9561792 |pmid=36250039 |archive-date=2023-11-22 |access-date=2023-11-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231122004404/https://ps.psychopen.eu/index.php/ps/article/view/7269 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Personality neuroscience is considered as an interdisciplinary field integrating research questions and methodologies from [[social psychology]], [[personality psychology]], and [[neuroscience]]. It is closely related to other interdisciplinary fields, such as [[Social neuroscience|social]], [[Cognitive neuroscience|cognitive]], and [[affective neuroscience]].

== History ==

Personality neuroscience is a field built upon the study of personality, which has been a central theme in psychology and evolving through various theoretical perspectives as well as methodological approaches over many years. Specifically, personality neuroscience aims to understand what neurobiological mechanisms underlie and contribute to personality, and therefore, is primarily based on theories that attribute individual differences to physiological and biological systems of the human body or brain. These theories can be traced back to many theories proposed by early physicians, philosophers, and psychologists.<ref name="John-2008">{{Cite book |last1=John |first1=Oliver P. |title=Handbook of personality: theory and research |last2=Robins |first2=Richard W. |last3=Pervin |first3=Lawrence A. |date=2008 |publisher=Guilford press |isbn=978-1-59385-836-0 |edition=3rd |location=New York}}</ref> Ancient Greek physician [[Hippocrates]] developed the theories of [[Humorism]] by identifying four vital bodily "humors" or fluids (i.e., blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) to be associated with temperaments (i.e., sanguine, phlegmatic, melancholic, and choleric, respectively) as well as physical health outcomes.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2020-03-26 |title=Humoral Theory |url=https://curiosity.lib.harvard.edu/contagion/feature/humoral-theory |access-date=2023-11-25 |website=Contagion - CURIOSity Digital Collections |language=en}}</ref> In the early 20th century, the psychoanalytic theories put forth by Austrian neurologist [[Sigmund Freud]] was anchored on the unconscious mental processes.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Safran |first1=J. D. |title=Psychoanalysis |date=2016-01-01 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123970459001890 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Mental Health (Second Edition) |pages=339–347 |editor-last=Friedman |editor-first=Howard S. |access-date=2023-11-26 |place=Oxford |publisher=Academic Press |doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-397045-9.00189-0 |isbn=978-0-12-397753-3 |last2=Gardner-Schuster |first2=E.|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Influenced by the psychoanalytic theories, American psychologist [[Henry Murray|Henry A. Murray]] proposed five principles of personology, his term for the study and system of personality, in which the first principle states that "personality is rooted in the brain. The individual's cerebral physiology guides and govern every aspect of personality". Relatedly, Murray also suggested that "needs", which is the motivation that drive behaviors, arose as a result of "a physiochemical force in the brain".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Murray |first=Henry Alexander |title=Exploration in Personality |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |year=1938}}</ref> American psychologist William Sheldon was known for his work on defining three "[[Somatotype and constitutional psychology|somatotypes]]" (i.e., body types: endomorphs, mesomorphs, and ectomorphs) to personality attributes.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=1940-10-12 |title=The Varieties of Human Physique: An Introduction to Constitutional Psychology |url=http://jama.jamanetwork.com/article.aspx?doi=10.1001/jama.1940.02810410069045 |journal=Journal of the American Medical Association |language=en |volume=115 |issue=15 |page=1303 |doi=10.1001/jama.1940.02810410069045 |issn=0002-9955|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

As early as the late 19th century, the case study of [[Phineas Gage]], a railroad worker who survived a severe brain injury from an accident and underwent a significant personality change, was the first to suggest a causal link between the brain and personality.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=MacMillan |first1=Malcom |title=An odd kind of fame: stories of Phineas Gage |last2=Gage |first2=Phineas |date=2002 |publisher=MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-63259-1 |series=A Bradford book |location=Cambridge, Mass.}}</ref> In the 1940s, there were studies investigating the association between brain wave patterns and individual differences using [[Twin study|twin study paradigms]], demonstrating that identical twins showed remarkably similar brain wave patterns measured by [[electroencephalography]] (EEG) when compared to fraternal twins.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gottlober |first=A. B. |date=1938 |title=The inheritance of brain potential patterns. |url=http://doi.apa.org/getdoi.cfm?doi=10.1037/h0055570 |journal=Journal of Experimental Psychology |language=en |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=193–200 |doi=10.1037/h0055570 |issn=0022-1015|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=1945 |title=The Brain-Wave Pattern, an Hereditary Trait |journal=Journal of Heredity |volume=36 |issue=8 |pages=233–243 |doi=10.1093/oxfordjournals.jhered.a105509 |issn=1465-7333 }}</ref> However, results from these studies were deemed hard to interpret "in the absence of any satisfactory theory linking brain-wave patterns to personality".<ref name="Eysenck-1951">{{Cite journal |last1=Eysenck |first1=H. J. |last2=Prell |first2=D. B. |date=1951 |title=The Inheritance of Neuroticism: An Experimental Study |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0368315X00171956/type/journal_article |journal=Journal of Mental Science |language=en |volume=97 |issue=408 |pages=441–465 |doi=10.1192/bjp.97.408.441 |pmid=14861606 |issn=0368-315X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Building off these studies and other studies that investigated the genetic inheritance of psychological attributes, in 1951, [[Hans Eysenck|Hans J. Eysenck]] and D.B. Prell experimentally tested the heredity of neuroticism using a twin study paradigm and concluded that "the factor of neuroticism is not a statistical [artifact], but constitutes a biological unit which is inherited as a whole" and "the neurotic predisposition is to a large extent hereditarily determined".<ref name="Eysenck-1951" /> Following this work, Eysenck continued to investigate psychological traits in relation to neurobiological systems, including the nervous systems, arousal, and brain structures (e.g., [[reticular formation]] and the [[limbic system]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eysenck |first=H. J. |date=1963 |title=Biological Basis of Personality |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/1991031a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=199 |issue=4898 |pages=1031–1034 |doi=10.1038/1991031a0 |pmid=14066934 |bibcode=1963Natur.199.1031E |s2cid=3213932 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Eysenck-1985">{{Cite book |last1=Eysenck |first1=Hans J. |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4613-2413-3 |title=Personality and Individual Differences |last2=Eysenck |first2=Michael W. |date=1985 |publisher=Springer US |isbn=978-1-4612-9470-2 |location=Boston, MA |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-2413-3|doi-broken-date=22 August 2026 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eysenck |first=Hans J. |date=1990 |title=Biological dimensions of personality |journal=[[Handbook of Personality: Theory and Research]] |pages=244–276}}</ref> In 1961, American psychologist [[Gordon Allport|Gordon W. Allport]] defined personality as "the dynamic organization within the individual of those psychophysical systems that determine his characteristic behavior and thought", localizing personality within "psychophysical systems".<ref name="Allport-1961">{{Cite book |last=Allport |first=Gordon W. |title=Pattern and growth in personality |date=1961 |publisher=Holt, Rinehart & Winston |isbn=978-0-03-010810-5 |series=Psychology |location=New York, NY}}</ref>

=== Development ===
Extending from Eysenck's theory on the biological basis of personality, [[Jeffrey Alan Gray|Jeffrey A. Gray]]'s [[reinforcement sensitivity theory]] of personality and his work that studied the neural mechanisms underlying personality traits set the foundation for the contemporary field in personality neuroscience.<ref name="Gray-1970">{{Cite journal |last=Gray |first=Jeffrey A. |date=1970-08-01 |title=The psychophysiological basis of introversion-extraversion |journal=Behaviour Research and Therapy |volume=8 |issue=3 |pages=249–266 |doi=10.1016/0005-7967(70)90069-0 |pmid=5470377 |issn=0005-7967}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Gray |first1=Jeffrey Alan |title=The neuropsychology of anxiety: an enquiry into the function of the septo-hippocampal system |last2=McNaughton |first2=Neil |date=2007 |publisher=Oxford Univ. Press |isbn=978-0-19-852271-3 |edition=2. ed., repr |series=Oxford psychology series |location=Oxford}}</ref> For example, Gray's work suggested that introversion involved both the ascending reticular activating system and an inhibitory system of brain areas including the orbital frontal cortex, medial septal area, and. the hippocampus.<ref name="Gray-1970" /> In 1999, a chapter titled "The neuroscience of personality" written by Alan D. Pickering and Jeffrey A. Gray was published in the ''Handbook of personality: Theory and research'', in which it introduced ways to "build a modern, integrated neuroscience of personality".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pickering |first1=Alan D. |last2=Gray |first2=Jeffrey A. |date=1999 |title=The neuroscience of personality |journal=[[Handbook of Personality: Theory and Research]] |pages=277–299}}</ref>

Although there had long been theoretically driven interests and experimental endeavors to understand the neurobiological basis of personality, it wasn't until recent years that, with the advancement in neuroscientific methodologies (e.g., non-invasive neuroimaging methods), the focus of personality psychology began to shift from observing, describing, and categorizing the phenomenon of individual differences towards discovering what may contribute to these observed individual differences.<ref name="DeYoung-2020">{{Citation |last1=DeYoung |first1=Colin G. |chapter=Personality Neuroscience |date=2020-09-03 |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/9781108264822%23CN-bp-20/type/book_part |title=The Cambridge Handbook of Personality Psychology |pages=273–292 |editor-last=Corr |editor-first=Philip J. |access-date=2023-11-23 |edition=2 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |doi=10.1017/9781108264822.026 |isbn=978-1-108-26482-2 |last2=Blain |first2=Scott D. |s2cid=262041010 |editor2-last=Matthews |editor2-first=Gerald|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref> In 2010, the name "personality neuroscience" was coined by [[Colin G. DeYoung]],<ref name="DeYoung-2010">{{Cite journal |last=DeYoung |first=Colin G. |date=2010 |title=Personality Neuroscience and the Biology of Traits: Personality Neuroscience |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1751-9004.2010.00327.x |journal=[[Social and Personality Psychology Compass]] |language=en |volume=4 |issue=12 |pages=1165–1180 |doi=10.1111/j.1751-9004.2010.00327.x|s2cid=15018241 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="DeYoung-2010-2">{{Cite journal |last1=DeYoung |first1=Colin G. |last2=Hirsh |first2=Jacob B. |last3=Shane |first3=Matthew S. |last4=Papademetris |first4=Xenophon |last5=Rajeevan |first5=Nallakkandi |last6=Gray |first6=Jeremy R. |date=2010 |title=Testing Predictions From Personality Neuroscience: Brain Structure and the Big Five |journal=Psychological Science |language=en |volume=21 |issue=6 |pages=820–828 |doi=10.1177/0956797610370159 |pmid=20435951 |pmc=3049165 |issn=0956-7976}}</ref> who is a psychology professor and the director of the [https://deyoung.psych.umn.edu DeYoung Personality Lab] at the University of Minnesota.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Colin DeYoung |url=https://cla.umn.edu/about/directory/profile/cdeyoung |access-date=2023-11-24 |website=College of Liberal Arts |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The DeYoung Personality Lab {{!}} DeYoung Personality Lab |url=https://deyoung.psych.umn.edu/ |access-date=2023-11-24 |website=deyoung.psych.umn.edu}}</ref> In 2018, the [https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/personality-neuroscience ''Personality Neuroscience'' journal] was established to "[publish] papers in the neuroscience of personality (including cognitive abilities, emotionality, and other individual differences) concerned with understanding causal bases" with "its focus on the equal importance of personality and neuroscience".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Personality Neuroscience {{!}} Cambridge Core |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/personality-neuroscience |access-date=2023-11-23 |website=Cambridge Core |language=en}}</ref>

== Research methodologies ==
As personality neuroscience seeks to understand the link between personality and its underlying neurobiological mechanisms, generating testable hypotheses involve both the measurements of personality attributes and neurobiological structures and/or functions.<ref name="DeYoung-2010" />

=== Measuring personality ===
In the field of personality psychology, there have been two main approaches to define personality traits:<ref name="John-2008" />

# '''Nomothetic approach''' defines personality traits in terms of dimensions and factors, or typologies comprising an organized group of trait-like characteristics, that are generalizable and universal to all people. Along with the development of the [[factor analysis]] and [[psychometrics]], the nomothetic approach has been dominant in personality psychology as it offers quantitative measures of traits that can be easily incorporated in research designs and statistical analyses. Two popular models of personality traits are Eysenck's [[Eysenck Personality Questionnaire|three-factor model]]<ref name="Eysenck-1985" /> (including three factors: neuroticism, extraversion, and psychoticism) and Goldberg's Big Five<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goldberg |first=Lewis R. |date=1990 |title=An alternative "description of personality": The Big-Five factor structure. |url=http://doi.apa.org/getdoi.cfm?doi=10.1037/0022-3514.59.6.1216 |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=59 |issue=6 |pages=1216–1229 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.59.6.1216 |pmid=2283588 |bibcode=1990JPSP...59.1216G |s2cid=9034636 |issn=0022-3514|url-access=subscription }}</ref> or McCrae and Costa's five-factor model<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=McCrae |first1=Robert R. |last2=John |first2=Oliver P. |date=1992 |title=An Introduction to the Five-Factor Model and Its Applications |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-6494.1992.tb00970.x |journal=Journal of Personality |language=en |volume=60 |issue=2 |pages=175–215 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-6494.1992.tb00970.x |pmid=1635039 |s2cid=10596836 |issn=0022-3506|url-access=subscription }}</ref> (including five factors: extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and impulsivity/openness), in which the latter two are made up of slightly different dimensions but often conceptualized interchangeably in the literature. Just as the Eysenck model and Golderberg/McCrae and Costa's model disagree fundamentally on the numbers of factors (three versus five, respectively), there exists ongoing debates about the numbers of orthogonal factors that may be sufficient to define the personality space.<ref name="John-2008" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eysenck |first=H. J. |date=1992-06-01 |title=Four ways five factors are not basic |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=667–673 |doi=10.1016/0191-8869(92)90237-J |issn=0191-8869}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Costa |first1=Paul T. |last2=McCrae |first2=Robert R. |date=1992-06-01 |title=Four ways five factors are basic |journal=Personality and Individual Differences |volume=13 |issue=6 |pages=653–665 |doi=10.1016/0191-8869(92)90236-I |s2cid=86867568 |issn=0191-8869}}</ref> In recent years, a hierarchal model of the Big Five personality<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Big Five Personality Hierarchy {{!}} DeYoung Personality Lab |url=https://deyoung.psych.umn.edu/big-five-hierarchy |access-date=2023-11-27 |website=deyoung.psych.umn.edu}}</ref> is proposed, grouping the five factors (or "domains") into two higher-order "metatraits": stability (i.e., agreeableness, conscientiousness, and reverse-coded neuroticism) and plasticity (i.e., extraversion and openness/intellect) while dividing each domain into two aspects associated with different facets.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=DeYoung |first=Colin G. |date=2006 |title=Higher-order factors of the Big Five in a multi-informant sample. |url=http://doi.apa.org/getdoi.cfm?doi=10.1037/0022-3514.91.6.1138 |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=91 |issue=6 |pages=1138–1151 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.91.6.1138 |pmid=17144770 |issn=1939-1315|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=DeYoung |first1=Colin G. |last2=Quilty |first2=Lena C. |last3=Peterson |first3=Jordan B. |date=2007 |title=Between facets and domains: 10 aspects of the Big Five. |url=http://doi.apa.org/getdoi.cfm?doi=10.1037/0022-3514.93.5.880 |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=93 |issue=5 |pages=880–896 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.93.5.880 |pmid=17983306 |bibcode=2007JPSP...93..880D |s2cid=8261816 |issn=1939-1315|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jang |first1=Kerry L. |last2=McCrae |first2=Robert R. |last3=Angleitner |first3=Alois |last4=Riemann |first4=Rainer |last5=Livesley |first5=W. John |date=1998 |title=Heritability of facet-level traits in a cross-cultural twin sample: Support for a hierarchical model of personality. |url=http://doi.apa.org/getdoi.cfm?doi=10.1037/0022-3514.74.6.1556 |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |language=en |volume=74 |issue=6 |pages=1556–1565 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.74.6.1556 |pmid=9654759 |issn=1939-1315|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 
# '''Idiographic approach''' emphasizes individuality and defines traits, including individualized traits and the pattern or organization of a combination of traits, in relation to a particular person. Allport, endorsing the idiographic approach, wrote that "''the outstanding characteristic of man is his individuality''", and his trait theory—centering on the cardinal, central, and secondary traits—were defined in idiographic terms.<ref name="Allport-1961" /> Personality research that adopted the idiographic approach have demonstrated that the nomothetic approach (e.g., the Big Five) may not be able to capture the within-person personality structure.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cervone |first=Daniel |date=2005-02-01 |title=Personality Architecture: Within-Person Structures and Processes |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.psych.56.091103.070133 |journal=Annual Review of Psychology |language=en |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=423–452 |doi=10.1146/annurev.psych.56.091103.070133 |pmid=15709942 |issn=0066-4308|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In personality neuroscience, personality is often defined using the nomothetic approach. Personality trait is typically measured using scales developed for the personality attributes of interests and administered through self-report surveys and questionnaires. One of the most commonly used ways to measure personality attributes in personality neuroscience research is the [[Big Five personality traits|Big-Five personality traits]]. In addition to the criticism by proponents of the idiographic approach as mentioned above, self-report measures on personality traits in general are susceptible to response biases (e.g., [[Social-desirability bias|social desirability bias]], [[Acquiescence bias|acquiescent response bias]], etc.) and inaccurate introspection of mental states. Therefore, it is important to establish construct validity of the self-report measures of personality by using other scales of the same construct or other modalities of measures, such as behavioral data or aggregated ratings from other knowledgeable informants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paulhus |first1=Delroy L. |last2=Vazire |first2=Simine |date=2009 |title=The Self-Report Method |journal=[[Handbook of Research Methods in Personality Psychology]] |pages=224–239}}</ref>

Another common nomothetic approach is the Affective Neuroscience Personality Scales (ANPS). The ANPS was originally published in 2003 and was used by neuroscientists to evaluate the primary emotional systems that underlie mental well-being and affective brain disorders.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Montag |first1=Christian |last2=Davis |first2=Kenneth L. |date=2018-08-10 |title=Affective Neuroscience Theory and Personality: An Update |journal=Personality Neuroscience |volume=1 |article-number=e12 |doi=10.1017/pen.2018.10 |issn=2513-9886 |pmc=7219919 |pmid=32435731}}</ref> This scale was created by [[Jaak Panksepp]] so that researchers could use this self-report test to measure differences in the primary emotions, SEEKING, LUST, CARE, PLAY (the positive emotions) and FEAR, SADNESS, ANGER (the negative emotions). These differences in the emotions were then compared to the Big Five personality to look at the scale from an evolutionary perspective as the primary emotions were seen as a survival mechanism of inherited behavioral patterns by humans interacting with their environment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Marengo |first1=Davide |last2=Davis |first2=Kenneth L. |last3=Gradwohl |first3=Gökçe Özkarar |last4=Montag |first4=Christian |date=2021 |title=A meta-analysis on individual differences in primary emotional systems and Big Five personality traits |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=7453 |doi=10.1038/s41598-021-84366-8  |doi-access=free|pmid=33811242|pmc=8018956 |bibcode=2021NatSR..11.7453M |hdl=2318/1829276 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> Each of these primary emotions have "been evolutionarily shaped in terms of inherited tools for survival and, more generally, for fitness" and are seen to regulate human nature.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brienza |first1=Lorenzo |last2=Zennaro |first2=Alessandro |last3=Vitolo |first3=Enrico |last4=Andò |first4=Agata |date=2023-01-01 |title=Affective Neuroscience Personality Scale (ANPS) and clinical implications: A systematic review |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165032722011107 |journal=Journal of Affective Disorders |volume=320 |pages=178–195 |doi=10.1016/j.jad.2022.09.104 |pmid=36174784 |issn=0165-0327|url-access=subscription |hdl=2318/1877276 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The SEEKING energy is used to seek valuable resources for survival, such as food, a mate, or shelter. The LUST energy is used to sustain the human species through reproductive means. The CARE system is significant in order to protect offspring so that they can grow into adults and the species is sustained once again. PLAY is important in order to foster social bonding between humans, to learn social and motor skills, and to regulate emotions. On the other hand with negative emotions, the FEAR energy is used for safety and to keep away from danger through means such as the flight or fight response. The SADNESS system, from an evolutionary perspective, is used to maintain socialness of an individual, as being isolated often evokes this emotion. The ANGER energy is important to protect resources from others or the environment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Montag |first1=Christian |last2=Elhai |first2=Jon D. |last3=Davis |first3=Kenneth L. |date=2021-06-01 |title=A comprehensive review of studies using the Affective Neuroscience Personality Scales in the psychological and psychiatric sciences |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763421000737 |journal=Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews |volume=125 |pages=160–167 |doi=10.1016/j.neubiorev.2021.02.019 |pmid=33609568 |issn=0149-7634|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

However, since the late 2010s, researchers have begun to question the relevancy of ANPS and have identified areas of improvement. The primary emotional systems in psychopathologies often fluctuate. The assessment is also only found in one long version, and patients with depression who suffer from fatigue would benefit from a shorter version. Furthermore, the FEAR and SADNESS emotions exhibit high correlation because they are closely related, and it would be useful to find a method to disentangle them to better study them. Another concern is that the original ANPS does not assess individual differences in LUST.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Montag |first1=Christian |last2=Solms |first2=Mark |last3=Stelzel |first3=Christine |last4=Davis |first4=Kenneth L. |date=2022-09-20 |title=The future of the Affective Neuroscience Personality Scales: A reflection on seven pressing matters |journal=Personality Neuroscience |volume=5 |article-number=e10 |doi=10.1017/pen.2022.2 |issn=2513-9886 |pmc=9549392 |pmid=36258778}}</ref>

=== Measuring brain structures and functions ===
To study the neurobiological mechanisms, or the structures and functions of the brain, underlying personality, personality neuroscience research employs established methods from [[neuroscience]] research. Some of the available neuroscientific methods are listed below with brief descriptions and how they can be incorporated in personality neuroscience research.<ref name="DeYoung-2020" />

'''[[Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain|Magnetic resonance imaging]] (MRI)''' is a non-invasive imaging technique that uses the physical properties of  magnetic fields and injection of radio-frequency pulses to examine the brain structure and functions with high spatial resolution.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Poldrack |first1=Russell A. |last2=Farah |first2=Martha J. |date=2015 |title=Progress and challenges in probing the human brain |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nature15692 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=526 |issue=7573 |pages=371–379 |doi=10.1038/nature15692 |pmid=26469048 |bibcode=2015Natur.526..371P |s2cid=4457455 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Both sMRI and fMRI have been used widely in both clinical and research settings to establish associations between the brain and a wide range of human socio-cognitive and psychological processes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lieberman |first=Matthew D. |date=2007-01-01 |title=Social Cognitive Neuroscience: A Review of Core Processes |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085654 |journal=Annual Review of Psychology |language=en |volume=58 |issue=1 |pages=259–289 |doi=10.1146/annurev.psych.58.110405.085654 |pmid=17002553 |issn=0066-4308|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Adolphs |first=Ralph |date=2009-01-01 |title=The Social Brain: Neural Basis of Social Knowledge |journal=Annual Review of Psychology |language=en |volume=60 |issue=1 |pages=693–716 |doi=10.1146/annurev.psych.60.110707.163514 |issn=0066-4308 |pmc=2588649 |pmid=18771388}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rilling |first1=James K. |last2=Sanfey |first2=Alan G. |date=2011-01-10 |title=The Neuroscience of Social Decision-Making |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/10.1146/annurev.psych.121208.131647 |journal=Annual Review of Psychology |language=en |volume=62 |issue=1 |pages=23–48 |doi=10.1146/annurev.psych.121208.131647 |pmid=20822437 |issn=0066-4308|hdl=2066/99774 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref> as well as individual differences.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dubois |first1=Julien |last2=Adolphs |first2=Ralph |date=June 2016 |title=Building a Science of Individual Differences from fMRI |journal=Trends in Cognitive Sciences |volume=20 |issue=6 |pages=425–443 |doi=10.1016/j.tics.2016.03.014 |issn=1364-6613 |pmc=4886721 |pmid=27138646}}</ref> Structural MRI (sMRI) of the brain provides the information on the neuroanatomical properties of the brain, such as the volumes of the [[Grey matter|gray]] and [[white matter]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Symms |first1=M. |last2=Jäger |first2=H. R. |last3=Schmierer |first3=K. |last4=Yousry |first4=T. A. |date=2004-09-01 |title=A review of structural magnetic resonance neuroimaging |url=https://jnnp.bmj.com/content/75/9/1235 |journal=Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry |language=en |volume=75 |issue=9 |pages=1235–1244 |doi=10.1136/jnnp.2003.032714 |issn=0022-3050 |pmc=1739217 |pmid=15314108}}</ref> Functional MRI (fMRI) of the brain maps the functional organization of the brain by monitoring the localized brain activation through the change in blood oxygenation level as a result of the cerebral blood flow (CBF), either when participants are engaging in tasks (i.e., task-based fMRI) or at rest (i.e., resting-state fMRI).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Glover |first=Gary H. |date=2011 |title=Overview of Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging |journal=Neurosurgery Clinics of North America |language=en |volume=22 |issue=2 |pages=133–139 |doi=10.1016/j.nec.2010.11.001 |pmc=3073717 |pmid=21435566}}</ref> In addition to examine brain structure and function within localized brain regions, topological network analyses, such as graph theory in network neuroscience, can be conducted across brain regions to map out structural and functional connectivity patterns that vary with inter-individual variation in cognition and behaviors.<ref name="Hilger-2021">{{Cite journal |last1=Hilger |first1=Kirsten |last2=Markett |first2=Sebastian |date=2021 |title=Personality network neuroscience: Promises and challenges on the way toward a unifying framework of individual variability |url= |journal=[[Network Neuroscience]] |volume=5 |issue=3 |language=en |pages=631–645 |doi=10.1162/netn_a_00198 |issn=2472-1751 |pmc=8567832 |pmid=34746620}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Park |first1=Hae-Jeong |last2=Friston |first2=Karl |date=2013 |title=Structural and Functional Brain Networks: From Connections to Cognition |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.1238411 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=342 |issue=6158 |article-number=1238411 |doi=10.1126/science.1238411 |pmid=24179229 |bibcode=2013Sci...34238411P |s2cid=17577672 |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In recent years, large MRI datasets, such as the Human Connectome Project (HCP), were collected with the aim to investigate the individual differences in structural and functional connectivity of the brain networks underlying a wide range of cognitive processes elicited by fMRI tasks.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barch |first1=Deanna M. |last2=Burgess |first2=Gregory C. |last3=Harms |first3=Michael P. |last4=Petersen |first4=Steven E. |last5=Schlaggar |first5=Bradley L. |last6=Corbetta |first6=Maurizio |last7=Glasser |first7=Matthew F. |last8=Curtiss |first8=Sandra |last9=Dixit |first9=Sachin |last10=Feldt |first10=Cindy |last11=Nolan |first11=Dan |last12=Bryant |first12=Edward |last13=Hartley |first13=Tucker |last14=Footer |first14=Owen |last15=Bjork |first15=James M. |date=2013 |title=Function in the human connectome: Task-fMRI and individual differences in behavior |journal=NeuroImage |language=en |volume=80 |pages=169–189 |doi=10.1016/j.neuroimage.2013.05.033 |pmc=4011498 |pmid=23684877}}</ref>

'''[[Positron emission tomography]] (PET)''' is an imaging technique that uses radiotracers to spatially localize and track the distribution of changes in metabolic processes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nasrallah |first1=Ilya |last2=Dubroff |first2=Jacob |date=2013-11-01 |title=An Overview of PET Neuroimaging |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001299813000561 |journal=Seminars in Nuclear Medicine |series=Non-Oncology PET (Part II) |volume=43 |issue=6 |pages=449–461 |doi=10.1053/j.semnuclmed.2013.06.003 |pmid=24094712 |issn=0001-2998|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Specifically, PET neuroimaging scans have  been widely used in pre-clinical and clinical settings in relation to epilepsy, dementia, Parkinson's disease, and traumatic brain injuries.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sarikaya |first=Ismet |date=2015 |title=PET studies in epilepsy |journal=American Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging |volume=5 |issue=5 |pages=416–430 |issn=2160-8407 |pmc=4620171 |pmid=26550535}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Phelps |first=Michael E. |date=2000 |title=Positron emission tomography provides molecular imaging of biological processes |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=97 |issue=16 |pages=9226–9233 |doi=10.1073/pnas.97.16.9226 |pmid=10922074 |pmc=16850 |issn=0027-8424 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

'''[[Electroencephalography]] (EEG)''' is a tool that directly measures and records the electrical activity generated in the brain with high temporal resolution but relatively low spatial resolution.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Srinivasan |first1=R. |title=Electroencephalography |date=2012-01-01 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780123750006003955 |encyclopedia=Encyclopedia of Human Behavior (Second Edition) |pages=15–23 |editor-last=Ramachandran |editor-first=V. S. |access-date=2023-11-25 |place=San Diego |publisher=Academic Press |doi=10.1016/b978-0-12-375000-6.00395-5 |isbn=978-0-08-096180-4 |last2=Nunez |first2=P. L.|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The EEG signal can be obtained non-invasively by placing electrodes on the scalp to capture the electrical impulses produced by neurons in the brain. It is commonly used in clinical settings to assess and detect neurological abnormalities in brain functions, such as epilepsy, sleep disorder, and brain injuries; in research, it has been used in couple with tasks to probe brain activities underlying various cognitive and emotional processes.<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://academic.oup.com/book/35515 |title=Niedermeyer's Electroencephalography |date=2017 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-022848-4 |editor-last=Schomer |editor-first=Donald L. |volume=1 |language=en |doi=10.1093/med/9780190228484.001.0001 |editor-last2=Lopes Da Silva |editor-first2=Fernando H.}}</ref>

'''[[Molecular genetics]]''' is a sub-field in biology that investigates the structure, expression, and functions of genes, informing brain development and functions at the level of the genome.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Keverne |first=Eric B. |date=1994-01-01 |title=Molecular genetic approaches to understanding brain development and behaviour |journal=Psychoneuroendocrinology |volume=19 |issue=5 |pages=407–414 |doi=10.1016/0306-4530(94)90028-0 |pmid=7938342 |s2cid=3082286 |issn=0306-4530}}</ref> In the context of personality neuroscience, methods in molecular genetics have been used to establish genetic underpinnings of personality traits.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Canli |first=Turhan |title=Biology of personality and individual differences |date=2006 |publisher=Guilford Press |isbn=978-1-59385-252-8 |location=New York, NY}}</ref>

'''[[Assay]]''' measures biological processes by detecting signals produced by reagents.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Sittampalam |first1=G. Sitta |title=Preface |date=2017-03-31 |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK92019/ |work=Assay Guidance Manual [Internet] |access-date=2023-11-26 |publisher=Eli Lilly & Company and the National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences |language=en |last2=Coussens |first2=Nathan P.}}</ref> It can be used to quantify "endogenous psychoactive substances or their byproducts" (e.g., levels of dopamine, oxytocin, serotonin, etc.) that have been associated with psychological processes which may contribute to personality trait development or psychopathology.<ref name="DeYoung-2020" />

'''[[Neuropharmacology|Neuropharmocological manipulation]]''' involves the use of medication to induce changes in neurochemical processes and has been primarily studied for neurological or psychiatric drug treatments.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Introduction to neuropsychopharmacology |date=2009 |publisher=Oxford university press |isbn=978-0-19-538053-8 |location=New York}}</ref> Personality neuroscience can incorporate neuropsychopharmocological manipulation to establish causal link between personality traits and specific neurochemical processes (e.g., induced manipulation on levels of dopamine).<ref name="DeYoung-2010" />

== Current research ==
In the past two decades, research in the field of personality neuroscience, utilizing neuroscientific methods outlined in the previous section, has identified neural mechanisms underlying a wide range of trait variables. This section reviews some of the major research findings in the field.<ref name="DeYoung-2022" /><ref name="DeYoung-2010" />

=== Big-five personality traits ===
* '''[[Neuroticism]]''' indicates the general proclivity to experience negative emotions and it is a risk factor as well as strong predictor for a wide range of psychopathology. People high in neuroticism may be extremely vulnerable to negative events and exhibit high levels of emotional instability, anxiety, moodiness, irritability, sadness, and so on. A line of neuroimaging studies have established association between neuroticism and brain activity in the amygdala, insula, anterior cingulate, and medial prefrontal cortex.<ref name="DeYoung-2010" /> Through methods that probe the molecular or neurochemical mechanisms, neuroticism has been linked differentially to baseline or stressor-related levels of the stress hormone cortisol, lower levels of serotonergic function, and higher levels of norepinephrine.<ref name="DeYoung-2010" /> EEG studies have demonstrated that withdraw-related neuroticism is correlated with greater activation in the right frontal lobe in comparison to the left,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shackman |first1=Alexander J. |last2=McMenamin |first2=Brenton W. |last3=Maxwell |first3=Jeffrey S. |last4=Greischar |first4=Lawrence L. |last5=Davidson |first5=Richard J. |date=2009 |title=Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortical Activity and Behavioral Inhibition |journal=Psychological Science |volume=20 |issue=12 |pages=1500–1506 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9280.2009.02476.x |pmid=19906125 |pmc=2858783 |issn=0956-7976}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Balonr |first=Richard |date=2006-06-01 |title=A Review of: "Psychobiology of Personality. Second Edition. Revised and Updated" |journal=Annals of Clinical Psychiatry |volume=18 |issue=3 |pages=206–207 |doi=10.1080/10401230600803412 |issn=1040-1237}}</ref> whereas the aspect of anger-proneness in neuroticism is related to greater activation in the left frontal lobe in comparison to the right.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Harmon-Jones |first1=Eddie |last2=Allen |first2=John J. B. |date=1998 |title=Anger and frontal brain activity: EEG asymmetry consistent with approach motivation despite negative affective valence. |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |volume=74 |issue=5 |pages=1310–1316 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.74.5.1310 |pmid=9599445 |issn=1939-1315}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harmon-Jones |first=Eddie |date=2004 |title=Contributions from research on anger and cognitive dissonance to understanding the motivational functions of asymmetrical frontal brain activity |journal=Biological Psychology |volume=67 |issue=1–2 |pages=51–76 |doi=10.1016/j.biopsycho.2004.03.003 |pmid=15130525 |s2cid=8137723 |issn=0301-0511}}</ref> 
* '''[[Extraversion and introversion|Extraversion]]''' captures the extent to which individuals are outgoing, assertive, sociable, gregarious, and enthusiastic. Extraverts thrive on social interactions with others and are inclined to engage in large social gatherings, whereas introverts may prefer to socialize in smaller groups or alone and engage in more solitary activities. A series of sMRI and fMRI studies have associated extraversion with the structure and function of brain regions that have been implicated in reward processing, including the medial orbitofrontal cortex, nucleus accumbens, amygdala, and striatum.<ref name="DeYoung-2010" /> EEG studies on extraversion showed converging results that extraversion was correlated with an event-related waveform reflecting "dopaminergic signaling of reward".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Smillie |first1=Luke D. |last2=Jach |first2=Hayley K. |last3=Hughes |first3=David M. |last4=Wacker |first4=Jan |last5=Cooper |first5=Andrew J. |last6=Pickering |first6=Alan D. |date=2019 |title=Extraversion and reward-processing: Consolidating evidence from an electroencephalographic index of reward-prediction-error |journal=Biological Psychology |volume=146 |article-number=107735 |doi=10.1016/j.biopsycho.2019.107735 |pmid=31352030 |s2cid=198965905 |issn=0301-0511}}</ref> Consistent with the evidence from MRI and EEG studies, neuropharmocological manipulation methods have shown that extraversion was moderated by dopaminergic drugs and that dopamine influences the pattern of cortical arousal in relation to extraversion.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wacker |first1=Jan |last2=Smillie |first2=Luke D. |date=2015 |title=Trait Extraversion and Dopamine Function |url=https://compass.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/spc3.12175 |journal=Social and Personality Psychology Compass |language=en |volume=9 |issue=6 |pages=225–238 |doi=10.1111/spc3.12175 |issn=1751-9004|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wacker |first1=Jan |last2=Chavanon |first2=Mira-Lynn |last3=Stemmler |first3=Gerhard |date=2006 |title=Investigating the dopaminergic basis of extraversion in humans: A multilevel approach. |journal=Journal of Personality and Social Psychology |volume=91 |issue=1 |pages=171–187 |doi=10.1037/0022-3514.91.1.171 |pmid=16834487 |issn=1939-1315}}</ref> 
* '''[[Openness to experience]]''' reflects an individual's inclination toward novelty, creativity, and intellectual curiosity. High scorers on openness to experience tend to be imaginative and open-minded, while low scorers on this trait may prefer a lifestyle of routine and familiarity. Recent work using the resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project has demonstrated that the individual functional connectivity matrices predicted openness to experience with accuracy almost on par with predictions for scores on intelligence tests, but not other four personality trait variables under the five-factor personality framework.<ref name="Dubois-2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Dubois |first1=Julien |last2=Galdi |first2=Paola |last3=Han |first3=Yanting |last4=Paul |first4=Lynn K. |last5=Adolphs |first5=Ralph |date=2018-07-05 |title=Resting-State Functional Brain Connectivity Best Predicts the Personality Dimension of Openness to Experience |journal=Personality Neuroscience |language=en |volume=1 |article-number=e6 |doi=10.1017/pen.2018.8 |issn=2513-9886 |pmc=6138449 |pmid=30225394}}</ref> In an fMRI study of older adults who underwent a visual memory encoding task in the scanner, a more similar functional memory brain-network activation patterns in older adults when compared to patterns in young adults, indicating a better preservation of the memory network, mediated the relationship between high openness scores and better memory performance. This result may suggest that openness to experience may serve as a protective factor against aging and memory deterioration.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Stolz |first1=Christopher |last2=Bulla |first2=Ariane |last3=Soch |first3=Joram |last4=Schott |first4=Björn H |last5=Richter |first5=Anni |date=2023-01-01 |title=Openness to Experience is associated with neural and performance measures of memory in older adults |journal=Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience |volume=18 |issue=1 |article-number=nsad041 |doi=10.1093/scan/nsad041 |issn=1749-5016 |pmc=10533339 |pmid=37632761}}</ref>
* '''[[Agreeableness]]''' is related to interpersonal and socio-behavioral tendencies, such as compassion, cooperation, and kindness. People who are high in agreeableness are more empathetic and cooperative in general, while low scorers may be more competitive, antisocial, or exploitative. Not often a trait of interest in the literature of personality neuroscience as the construct is "social" in its nature, agreeableness has been linked to neural activity in left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex implicated in emotion regulation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Haas |first1=Brian W. |last2=Omura |first2=Kazufumi |last3=Constable |first3=R. Todd |last4=Canli |first4=Turhan |date=2007 |title=Is Automatic Emotion Regulation Associated With Agreeableness? |journal=Psychological Science |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=130–132 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01861.x |pmid=17425532 |s2cid=38049443 |issn=0956-7976}}</ref> In addition, one sMRI study has illustrated the correlation between agreeableness and volumes of brain areas that have been linked to social information processing (i.e., superior temporal sulcus, posterior cingulate cortex, and fusiform gyrus).<ref name="DeYoung-2010-2" /> 
* '''[[Conscientiousness]]''' encompasses traits related to self-discipline, organization, and dependability. Individuals high in conscientiousness are often goal-oriented, diligent, organized, and reliable, while those low in this trait may be more spontaneous and flexible. One sMRI study have discovered the association between conscientiousness and the volume of the middle frontal gyrus in lateral prefrontal cortex.<ref name="DeYoung-2010-2" /> In addition to the association with volume in the middle frontal gyrus, another sMRI study also found the correlation between conscientiousness and the volume of bilateral superior parietal lobe, and that trait conscientiousness mediated the relationship between these brain regions and academic performance.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Song |last2=Zhao |first2=Yajun |last3=Li |first3=Jingguang |last4=Wang |first4=Xu |last5=Luo |first5=Kui |last6=Gong |first6=Qiyong |date=2019-08-21 |title=Brain structure links trait conscientiousness to academic performance |journal=Scientific Reports |language=en |volume=9 |issue=1 |page=12168 |doi=10.1038/s41598-019-48704-1  |doi-access=free|issn=2045-2322 |pmc=6704183 |pmid=31434943|bibcode=2019NatSR...912168W }}</ref> Additionally, one fMRI study, which examined the functional connectivity within and across brain regions, identified a goal priority brain network (GPN) and its 5 sub-components. Functional connectivity within one GPN component (including regions of anterior insula, dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex) as well as the functional connectivity between this one component and other 4 sub-components within the GPN network, was significantly related to conscientiousness ratings.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rueter |first1=Amanda R. |last2=Abram |first2=Samantha V. |last3=MacDonald |first3=Angus W. |last4=Rustichini |first4=Aldo |last5=DeYoung |first5=Colin G. |date=2018 |title=The goal priority network as a neural substrate of Conscientiousness |journal=Human Brain Mapping |language=en |volume=39 |issue=9 |pages=3574–3585 |doi=10.1002/hbm.24195 |doi-access=free |issn=1065-9471 |pmc=6200659 |pmid=29691946}}</ref>

=== Empathy ===
Empathy, in the discussion here as a stable trait as in empathetic ability or capacity, can be defined as an affective response that "is similar to one's perception (directly experienced or imagined) and understanding (cognitive empathy) of the stimulus emotion, with recognition that the source of the emotion is not one's own", although there is still ongoing debate in the field on how to best define empathy.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cuff |first1=Benjamin M.P. |last2=Brown |first2=Sarah J. |last3=Taylor |first3=Laura |last4=Howat |first4=Douglas J. |date=2016 |title=Empathy: A Review of the Concept |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1754073914558466 |journal=Emotion Review |language=en |volume=8 |issue=2 |pages=144–153 |doi=10.1177/1754073914558466 |s2cid=147125172 |issn=1754-0739|url-access=subscription }}</ref> One sMRI study has demonstrated that inter subject variability in different facets of empathy is linked to neuroanatomical variation across different brain regions, such that (1) affective empathic abilities towards others were negatively correlated with the gray matter volumes of the precuneus, inferior frontal gyrus, and anterior cingulate, (2) cognitive perspective taking abilities were positively correlated with the gray matter volume of the anterior cingulate, and (3) the ability to empathize with fictional characters was positively linked to gray matter changes in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Banissy |first1=Michael J. |last2=Kanai |first2=Ryota |last3=Walsh |first3=Vincent |last4=Rees |first4=Geraint |date=2012-09-01 |title=Inter-individual differences in empathy are reflected in human brain structure |journal=NeuroImage |volume=62 |issue=3 |pages=2034–2039 |doi=10.1016/j.neuroimage.2012.05.081 |issn=1053-8119 |pmc=3778747 |pmid=22683384}}</ref> A meta-analysis of a series of fMRI studies have revealed that, when humans engage in empathetic processes, a network of brain regions are engaged, encompassing the insula, inferior frontal gyrus, medial frontal regions around the cingulate cortex, amygdala, thalamus, putamen, caudate, and primary somatosensory area SI.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Keysers |first1=Christian |last2=Gazzola |first2=Valeria |date=2009-12-01 |title=Expanding the mirror: vicarious activity for actions, emotions, and sensations |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0959438809001433 |journal=Current Opinion in Neurobiology |series=Motor systems • Neurology of behaviour |volume=19 |issue=6 |pages=666–671 |doi=10.1016/j.conb.2009.10.006 |pmid=19880311 |s2cid=2692907 |issn=0959-4388|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In addition to MRI studies, neuromodulation on mice and monkeys have shown that interference with oxytocin signaling causally influences empathy-related phenomena.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Paradiso |first1=Enrica |last2=Gazzola |first2=Valeria |last3=Keysers |first3=Christian |date=2021-06-01 |title=Neural mechanisms necessary for empathy-related phenomena across species |journal=Current Opinion in Neurobiology |series=The Social Brain |volume=68 |pages=107–115 |doi=10.1016/j.conb.2021.02.005 |pmid=33756399 |s2cid=232283263 |issn=0959-4388|doi-access=free |hdl=20.500.11755/5bac6361-888b-45d7-8ab7-b3f73cb5d28d |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

=== Genetic Factors ===
Prior research focused primarily on the causes of specific traits like extraversion, but 2018 research indicated that these individual traits do not alone determine personality. Researchers looked into the genes that are related to human personality. They identified the genes that interact with each other and one's environment to create personality. Around 1000 of such genes that affect temperament and character were found. This was further studied by looking at 1000 people in Germany and a 1000 people in Korea, and they found that in both countries and cultures, the genes for personality were all expressed in the brain. Around 33% of the genes were involved in the expression of temperament and character, while 67% of the genes were involved in either one or the other. These genes for character were expressed primarily in the brain circuits that regulate complex cognitive processes, such as goal seeking, conflict solving, and self-awareness. The genes were found to affect temperament and were expressed primarily in the habit learning pathways. Through these studies, these researchers were able to determine that the components of personality are numerous complex profiles. They also found that many molecular pathways can cause the exact same personality trait. Furthermore, environmental influences had small interactions with the genes for temperament and character but still had significant influence.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Garcia |first1=Danilo |chapter=The Future of Personality Research and Applications: Some Latest Findings |date=2019 |title=Personality and Brain Disorders: Associations and Interventions |pages=283–297 |editor-last=Garcia |editor-first=Danilo  |series=Contemporary Clinical Neuroscience |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-90065-0_13 |isbn=978-3-319-90065-0 |last2=Cloninger |first2=Kevin M. |last3=Lester |first3=Nigel |last4=Cloninger |first4=C. Robert |editor2-last=Archer |editor2-first=Trevor |editor3-last=Kostrzewa |editor3-first=Richard M.}}</ref>

== Challenges and future directions ==
As an interdisciplinary field that lie between personality psychology and neuroscience, personality neuroscience research may benefit both fields by informing the formation of neuroscience hypotheses and helping interpret findings through theoretical framework developed in personality psychology, and in turn, developing and refining personality models and theories with an enhanced understanding of underlying neurobiological mechanisms.<ref name="DeYoung-2010" /> Nonetheless, in the meantime, the interdisciplinary nature aggregates paradigmatic and methodological challenges from both fields.<ref name="DeYoung-2010" /><ref name="Hilger-2021" />

One prominent challenge for neuroimaging studies that aim to investigate individual differences is the low statistical power as a result of small sample sizes due to the high cost of data collection.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cremers |first1=Henk R. |last2=Wager |first2=Tor D. |last3=Yarkoni |first3=Tal |date=2017-11-20 |title=The relation between statistical power and inference in fMRI |journal=PLOS ONE |language=en |volume=12 |issue=11 |article-number=e0184923 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0184923 |issn=1932-6203 |pmc=5695788 |pmid=29155843 |bibcode=2017PLoSO..1284923C |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Poldrack |first1=Russell A. |last2=Baker |first2=Chris I. |last3=Durnez |first3=Joke |last4=Gorgolewski |first4=Krzysztof J. |last5=Matthews |first5=Paul M. |last6=Munafò |first6=Marcus R. |last7=Nichols |first7=Thomas E. |last8=Poline |first8=Jean-Baptiste |last9=Vul |first9=Edward |last10=Yarkoni |first10=Tal |date=2017 |title=Scanning the horizon: towards transparent and reproducible neuroimaging research |journal=Nature Reviews Neuroscience |language=en |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=115–126 |doi=10.1038/nrn.2016.167 |issn=1471-003X |pmc=6910649 |pmid=28053326}}</ref> Personality neuroscience research can thus benefit from data-sharing among studies and collective efforts to aggregate large neuroimaging datasets that include personality measures, such as the Human Connectome Project (HCP) and the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study.<ref name="DeYoung-2022" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mar |first1=Raymond A. |last2=Spreng |first2=R. Nathan |last3=DeYoung |first3=Colin G. |date=2013-09-01 |title=How to produce personality neuroscience research with high statistical power and low additional cost |journal=Cognitive, Affective, & Behavioral Neuroscience |language=en |volume=13 |issue=3 |pages=674–685 |doi=10.3758/s13415-013-0202-6 |pmid=23982973 |s2cid=256204634 |issn=1531-135X}}</ref><ref name="Dubois-2018" /> Ongoing effort to collect data from more diverse sample is also recommended to allow for generalization of study results to a larger population or investigation of similarities/differences among diverse communities.<ref name="DeYoung-2010" />

Another challenge is to establish reliable, systematic, and high-quality measurement of personality traits.<ref name="Markett-2018" /> Unlike intelligence tests that are performance-based, personality questionnaires are susceptible to biases as mentioned in earlier sections. As the theories of personality psychology continues to evolve and develop, extensive psychometric research may need to be conducted on various types of scales or assessments that are used to measure psychological traits to ensure that they produce reliable measures of personality variables of interest.<ref name="DeYoung-2022" />

One other challenge is that personality neuroscience is a relatively young field. Because of this, many of the previously published studies may be proven to be false positives due to under-powered studies that use small samples. Larger sample sizes are needed to detect smaller effects, which are common in personality neuroscience. A sample size of around 200 is needed to have 80% power and detect a correlation .2, which is often the average effect size in personality neuroscience. Thus, larger sample sizes are a needed change for this field.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=DeYoung |first1=Colin G. |last2=Beaty |first2=Roger E. |last3=Genç |first3=Erhan |last4=Latzman |first4=Robert D. |last5=Passamonti |first5=Luca |last6=Servaas |first6=Michelle N. |last7=Shackman |first7=Alexander J. |last8=Smillie |first8=Luke D. |last9=Spreng |first9=R. Nathan |last10=Viding |first10=Essi |last11=Wacker |first11=Jan |date=2022 |title=Personality Neuroscience: An Emerging Field with Bright Prospects |journal=Personality Science |volume=3 |article-number=e7269 |doi=10.5964/ps.7269 |issn=2700-0710 |pmc=9561792 |pmid=36250039}}</ref>

The complexity of both the brain and personality traits poses additional challenge to the interdisciplinary field of personality neuroscience which studies the relationship between these two complex systems.<ref name="DeYoung-2010" /> Current research suggests that there exists no one-to-one mapping between neurobiological and personality variables: multiple brain regions or neurochemical processes may underlie one trait variable, while in turn, one brain region or neurochemical processes may be instrumental for several cognitive and affective processes that may influence multiple traits. As a result, personality network neuroscience approaches, integrating quantitative methodologies from network analysis, have been proposed to encode the complex nature of both neural mechanisms and personality variables as networks to facilitate the investigation the brain-personality relationship.<ref name="Hilger-2021" /><ref name="Markett-2018">{{Cite journal |last1=Markett |first1=Sebastian |last2=Montag |first2=Christian |last3=Reuter |first3=Martin |date=2018 |title=Network Neuroscience and Personality |journal=Personality Neuroscience |language=en |volume=1 |article-number=e14 |doi=10.1017/pen.2018.12 |issn=2513-9886 |pmc=7219685 |pmid=32435733}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tompson |first1=Steven H. |last2=Falk |first2=Emily B. |last3=Vettel |first3=Jean M. |last4=Bassett |first4=Danielle S. |date=2018-07-02 |title=Network Approaches to Understand Individual Differences in Brain Connectivity: Opportunities for Personality Neuroscience |journal=Personality Neuroscience |language=en |volume=1 |article-number=e5 |doi=10.1017/pen.2018.4 |issn=2513-9886 |pmc=6133307 |pmid=30221246}}</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Personality psychology
